papers.title: Acetylation of NDUFA13 at K7 Senses OXPHOS Dysfunction to Disrupt Prohibitin Scaffolds and Drive Cristae Remodelling in Heart Failure
papers.authors: Nan, J.; Yang, X.; Lin, Y.; Shen, J.; Chen, H.; Xu, Z.; Ye, J.; Wang, Y.; Xiong, D.; Ke, C.; Zhu, L.; Kong, X.; Zhong, Z.; Ren, T.; Jiang, J.; Wang, X.; Wang, B.; Zhao, D.; Li, Z.-z.; Shao, Z.; Liu, B.; He, X.
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial cristae disintegration is a hallmark of heart failure, yet how oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) dysfunction triggers this structural collapse remains unclear. Here we identify acetylation of the complex I subunit NDUFA13 at lysine 7 (K7) as a metabolic sensor coupling OXPHOS dysfunction to cristae remodelling. OXPHOS inhibition drove NDUFA13-K7 hyperacetylation, inducing conformational compaction and translocation to the intermembrane space. Acetylated NDUFA13 competitively engaged PHB2 through its coiled-coil domain, displacing PHB1 and disassembling prohibitin scaffolds. The acetylation-mimetic NDUFA13-K7Q induced cristae fragmentation in vitro, and cardiomyocyte-specific K7Q knock-in mice showed accelerated mortality and cristae loss under pressure overload, accompanied by impaired TCA cycle flux, defective fatty acid oxidation and selective depletion of polyunsaturated cardiolipins. These findings establish NDUFA13-K7 acetylation as a reversible switch converting bioenergetic failure into pathological cristae remodelling and metabolic reprogramming, highlighting therapeutic potential for targeted deacetylation.

papers.title: Ginsenoside Rg1 Alleviates Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease Partially Through Regulating ABCB1‐Mediated Mitochondrial Dysfunction
papers.authors: Wenhui Xu; Jinghong Ye; Kezhou Dong; Zhendong Cao; Yimin Zhu; Lei Li; Baoju Huang
papers.venue: Journal of Biochemical and Molecular Toxicology
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT To investigate the protective effects of ginsenoside Rg1 on lung injury in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and to elucidate the underlying mechanism involving ATP‐binding cassette subfamily B member 1 (ABCB1)‐mediated regulation of mitochondrial function. A COPD rat model was established by cigarette smoke exposure, followed by in vivo administration of different doses of ginsenoside Rg1. ABCB1 knockdown was achieved by tail vein injection of short hairpin RNA (shRNA). Hematoxylin and eosin (HE) and Masson staining were performed to evaluate lung histopathology and collagen deposition. Pulmonary function was assessed by measuring inspiratory resistance (Ri), dynamic lung compliance (Cdyn), and the ratio of forced expiratory volume at 0.3 s to forced vital capacity (FEV 0 . 3 /FVC). In vitro, cigarette smoke extract (CSE) was used to induce injury in human bronchial epithelial (HBE) cells, followed by Rg1 treatment and ABCB1 overexpression or knockdown. Advanced glycation end products–receptor for advanced glycation end products (AGEs–RAGE) and early growth response protein 1–c‐Jun N‐terminal kinase (EGR1–JNK) signaling pathways were detected. In COPD rats, Rg1 markedly attenuated alveolar structural destruction and collagen deposition, decreased Ri, increased Cdyn and FEV 0 . 3 /FVC. ABCB1 knockdown partially reversed these protective effects. In HBE cells, Rg1 enhanced cell viability, restored mitochondrial membrane potential, reduced apoptosis, decreased ROS accumulation, and rescued intracellular ATP depletion. Rg1 inhibited the activation of the AGEs–RAGE and EGR1–JNK pathways in a manner associated with upregulation of ABCB1 expression. Ginsenoside Rg1 enhances mitochondrial function partially through upregulation of ABCB1 expression, thereby alleviating mitochondrial dysfunction in COPD rats and CSE‐treated HBE cells.

papers.title: Lipid‐matrix‐dependent effects of ceramide enrichment on cholesterol‐containing PSM and DLPC membranes
papers.authors: Eun Sub Song; Taejin Kwon
papers.venue: Bulletin of the Korean Chemical Society
papers.abstract: Abstract Ceramide is a bioactive sphingolipid that can reorganize cholesterol‐containing membranes, but how membrane properties change with increasing ceramide content in different lipid matrices remains unclear. Using Martini 3 coarse‐grained molecular dynamics simulations, we examine cholesterol‐containing PSM and DLPC membranes across a controlled palmitoyl ceramide (PCER) composition series at a single liquid‐phase temperature. Increasing PCER fraction generally decreases area per lipid and increases lipid ordering, consistent with membrane condensation. However, the responses differ between matrices. In PSM/CHOL, PCER is accommodated within an already ordered environment, producing only modest membrane stiffening. In DLPC/CHOL, PCER leads to greater changes in local packing heterogeneity and lateral organization, accompanied by a nonmonotonic mechanical response. PCER enrichment also changes the positional and orientational distributions of cholesterol in a matrix‐dependent manner. These results show that ceramide‐induced condensation does not necessarily produce monotonic membrane stiffening and highlight the importance of the host lipid matrix in determining membrane structure and mechanics.

papers.title: Mitochondrial ROS and Mitophagy in Intervertebral Disc Degeneration: Mechanistic Interplay and Links to Regulated Cell Death
papers.authors: Lice Wang; Kai Cao; Haozhe Cheng; Zhong Fang
papers.abstract: Intervertebral disc degeneration (IVDD) develops through interacting mechanical, matrix, nutritional, inflammatory and age-related processes. Mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) and mitophagy participate in some of these contexts, but current evidence does not place mitophagy failure at the start of every degenerative trajectory. Most mechanistic studies have been performed in nucleus pulposus (NP) cells. In these models, mechanical overload, inflammatory mediators and oxidant stress can depolarize mitochondria, disturb fission–fusion balance and increase mtROS. Mitophagy can limit injury when damaged cargo is selected and delivered through a competent lysosomal pathway; accumulation of pathway markers during blocked flux, or mitochondrial clearance that is not matched by renewal, need not be protective. The most extensive mechanistic literature concerns apoptosis and senescence. Evidence linking mitochondrial quality control to pyroptosis and ferroptosis is growing but remains model-dependent, whereas direct evidence for necroptosis is comparatively sparse. We use a capacity-matching framework to organize these findings around damage burden, cargo selection, lysosomal completion and mitochondrial renewal within the regional metabolic constraints of the disc. This is an interpretive framework rather than a newly identified pathway. Its purpose is to define testable conditions under which mitophagy is likely to be protective, insufficient or maladaptive, while preserving the distinction between NP-derived evidence and the more limited evidence from annulus fibrosus and cartilage endplate cells.

papers.title: PIrates of the vacuole: phosphoinositide hijacking by T4SS intracellular pathogens.
papers.authors: Matteo Bonazzi
papers.abstract: Intracellular bacteria equipped with a Type IV Secretion Systems (T4SS), including Legionella pneumophila, Coxiella burnetii, Brucella abortus, and Anaplasma/Ehrlichia species, evolved a convergent strategy of exploiting host cell lipids at every stage of infection, from cholesterol-rich raft-mediated entry to the establishment of replicative vacuoles that evade lysosomal destruction. Indeed, these pathogens actively remodel host cell membranes by deploying T4SS effectors that bind, generate, or deplete specific lipid species, in particular phosphoinositides and cholesterol, to dictate the identity and trafficking fate of their containing vacuole. A remarkable diversity of effectors with lipid-binding or lipid-modifying activities has now been characterized across these pathogens: from the PI4P-centric Dot/Icm effector cascade of Legionella to the cooperating CvpB, CvpE, and Vice triad of Coxiella, and the phosphoinositide-binding immune evasion effector BtpA of Brucella. These pathogens also tap into host lipid droplets for energy and membrane precursors, modulate bioactive lipid mediators such as prostaglandins to curb immune clearance, and present atypical surface lipids to minimize pattern recognition. Advances in lipidomics, including a landmark systematic identification of novel α-helical PI-binding effector folds conserved across Legionella and Coxiella, have shed new light on these processes with unprecedented resolution. This review examines the shared and divergent lipid-subversion strategies of T4SS-bearing intracellular pathogens from an integrated molecular, cellular, and lipidomic perspective, and highlights emerging opportunities for host-directed therapeutic intervention.

papers.title: Polymer-specific nanoplastic exposure, mitochondrial dysfunction, and depressed ejection fraction in humans
papers.authors: Alberta Maria Maddalena Palazzo; Lucia Scisciola; Manuela Giovanna Basilicata; Nunzia D’Onofrio; Pasquale Paolisso; Angelo Fenti; Francesco Prattichizzo; Celestino Sardu; Eduardo Sommella; Valentina Golino; Marta Belmonte; Asad Zia; Claudio Marra; Cristiano Amarelli; Laura Graciotti; Gianluca Fulgenzi; Fabiola Olivieri; Rosalba La Grotta; Antonio Ceriello; Maria Luisa Balestrieri; Bruno D’Agostino; Carmine Lubritto; Pasquale Iovino; Claudio Napoli; Pietro Campiglia; Emanuele Barbato; Philip Landrigan; Michelangela Barbieri; Raffaele Marfella; Giuseppe Paolisso
papers.abstract: Abstract Aims Micro- and nanoplastics (MNPs) are increasingly found in humans, but cardiac and energetic effects are unclear. Methods and Results In older adults without major comorbidities, blood levels of PS/PE were quantified, and left ventricular ejection fraction (EF) was measured by transthoracic echocardiography. To investigate polymer-specific cardiotoxic mechanisms, human AC16 cardiomyocytes were exposed to PS- or PE-nanoplastics. Mitochondrial function was assessed using Seahorse XF analysis, and molecular remodeling was characterized using transcriptomics and label-free quantitative proteomics. In humans, circulating PS and PE levels were each associated with EF in univariable analyses. PS and PE concentrations were higher in participants with EF <50% than in those with EF ≥50% (PE p=0.021; PS p<0.001). After multivariable adjustment for anthropometric and metabolic determinants of systolic function, PS remained independently associated with EF. In vitro, both polymers accumulated intracellularly and elicited mitochondrial stress. Chronic PS exposure induced a loss of respiratory capacity and bioenergetic reserve, with suppression of basal and maximal respiration and markedly reduced spare respiratory capacity. PE exposure produced a distinct remodeling pattern characterized by reduced maximal respiration, but increased ATP-linked respiration and tighter respiratory coupling, consistent with a compensatory state of reduced metabolic flexibility. Transcriptomic profiling revealed polymer-specific transcriptional phenotypes, with PE driving broader repression of cardiomyocyte structural, electrophysiological, and mitochondrial gene programs, whereas PS triggered a more restricted but coherent response. Proteomic profiling further identified a mitochondria-centered injury signature involving disruption of mitochondrial protein import and cristae organization, impairment of oxidative metabolism, altered redox buffering, and incomplete activation of mitochondrial quality-control pathways. Conclusions Nanoplastic exposure is associated with left ventricular systolic function in humans and induces polymer-specific cardiomyocyte remodeling in vitro. PS is strongly linked to systolic impairment, consistent with a mitochondria-centered cardiotoxic phenotype. These findings identify nanoplastics as a previously unrecognized environmental determinant of myocardial vulnerability and support polymer-specific risk stratification.

papers.title: Sfh3 is a sterol-modulated PI/PI4P transfer protein that confers azole resistance in yeast by specifically mediating lanosterol/PI exchange
papers.authors: Hamaï, A.; Perne, P.; Tripathi, A.; Syska, C.; Cardinal, A.; Delfosse, V.; Copic, A.; Murugan, N. A.; Debayle, D.; Drin, G.
papers.abstract: Lipid transfer proteins precisely distribute lipids within eukaryotic cells, supporting functions such as vesicular trafficking and cellular signaling. Here, we analyzed whether Sfh3 (Sec14 homolog 3) functions as a sterol/phosphatidylinositol (PI) exchanger to clarify its role in neutral lipid mobilization from lipid droplets and in azole resistance in yeast. Using real-time assays, we found that its ergosterol transfer capacity is not activated by PI and is inhibited by ergosterol biosynthesis intermediates, such as lanosterol. Next, we found that Sfh3 exhibits both PI and PI4P transfer activities, which sterols can modulate. Through kinetic, structure-function, and thermal stability analyses, we identified remarkable Sfh3 mutants and ranked Sfh3's relative affinity for its lipid ligands. This allowed us to show that Sfh3 performs selective lanosterol/PI exchange, provided it recognizes PI, in the presence of ergosterol, and that this activity is necessary for yeast resistance to miconazole. Collectively, our data show that Sfh3 is a sterol-regulated PI/PI4P transfer protein, potentially linking sterol metabolism and PI4P signaling during lipid droplet utilization. In azole-treated yeast, elevated lanosterol levels may shift Sfh3 into an exclusive PI/lanosterol exchange mode, promoting cellular detoxification and conferring drug resistance. By revealing unanticipated Sfh-mediated lipid transfer mechanisms, our study provides new insights into the Sec14 family.

papers.title: Synergistic regulation of neuroinflammation by mitophagy and the cGAS–STING pathway following ischemic stroke
papers.authors: Yu Xiao; Peijie Fu; Chun Zhao; Wenqi Song; Yutao Lu; Huiqin Wang; Xiaoping Yin; Zhiying Chen; Yuanyuan Xiang
papers.abstract: Neuroinflammation is widely recognized as a major driver of secondary brain injury following ischemic stroke. Recent studies have shown that mitochondrial dysfunction-induced mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) release is one of the key mechanisms activating the cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) pathway. Mitophagy, as a quality control mechanism maintaining mitochondrial homeostasis, selectively clears damaged mitochondria, thereby limiting the leakage of abnormal mtDNA. Although previous reviews have outlined the general framework of the mitophagy-cGAS-STING interaction in neuroinflammation, this review places it within the specific context of ischemic stroke. It integrates the cell type-specificity of the neurovascular unit, explores both synergistic and interactive aspects, and evaluates targeted nanotherapeutic strategies. This article aims to explore the potential synergistic role of mitophagy and the cGAS-STING pathway in the pathological progression of ischemic stroke. First, the article elaborates on mitophagy and mitophagy-dependent regulation of neuroinflammation, highlighting its role in suppressing cGAS-STING activation by preventing mtDNA leakage. Second, it examines the cGAS-STING signaling pathway in neuroinflammation, with particular attention to cGAS-STING activation across neurovascular unit cell types (microglia, neurons, astrocytes, endothelial cells). Third, the functional synergy and potential molecular crosstalk between mitophagy and the cGAS–STING pathway in neuroinflammation are discussed. Finally, the article summarizes the potential therapeutic strategies targeting mitophagy and the cGAS-STING pathway, and further explores the emerging potential of microenvironment-responsive intelligent nanoplatforms to enhance drug delivery efficiency and multidimensional synergistic mechanisms by targeting the cGAS-STING pathway and mitochondria, thereby achieving precise immune regulation and improving therapeutic efficacy. This paper provides a mechanistic perspective on immune intervention for ischemic stroke and lays a theoretical foundation for future clinical translation strategies.

papers.title: Triglycerides, Total Cholesterol, and Body Weight Index Demonstrates High Discriminative Performance for Metabolic Syndrome: A Comparative Study with Established Cardiometabolic and Inflammatory Indices
papers.authors: Mehmet Erdem; Tuğba Raika Kıran; Lezan Keskin; Süleyman Caner Karahan
papers.abstract: Objective: This research sought to assess the effectiveness of combined inflammatory and cardiometabolic markers, with a particular focus on the triglycerides, total cholesterol, and body weight index (TCBI), in individuals diagnosed with metabolic syndrome (MetS). Methods: This retrospective, single-center study included individuals aged 18-65 years who were admitted to the internal medicine clinic between January 2023 and January 2026. MetS was defined according to NCEP ATP III criteria. Demographic, anthropometric, and laboratory data were obtained from electronic medical records. In addition to routine biochemical and hematological parameters, composite indices including TCBI, TyG, CMI, CRP/HDL, NHR, UHR, NLAR, PIV, HALP, NLR, SIRI, and SII were calculated using standard formulas. Appropriate statistical tests were utilized to compare groups. To evaluate the diagnostic effectiveness of the indices, a ROC curve analysis was performed. Results: Several anthropometric and metabolic parameters differed significantly between groups (p < 0.05). Among the evaluated indices, TCBI, CMI, TyG, CRP/HDL, NHR, and UHR levels were significantly elevated in MetS patients (p < 0.0001), whereas NLAR, PIV, HALP, NLR, SIRI, and SII showed no significant differences (p > 0.05). ROC analysis demonstrated that TCBI had the highest diagnostic performance (AUC: 0.9622, 95% CI: 0.9378 - 0.9865, p < 0.0001), followed by CMI (AUC: 0.9600) and TyG (AUC: 0.9463). CRP/HDL, NHR, and UHR exhibited moderate discriminative ability. Conclusion: TCBI showed strong diagnostic performance in this cohort and demonstrated higher overall discriminative ability compared with the evaluated indices. These findings suggest that TCBI may represent a simple and accessible marker for MetS assessment. However, further studies are required to validate its clinical utility.

papers.title: A novel function of neuroligin 3: Beyond sociality, Regulating lifespan in Drosophila
papers.authors: Jurbaj, J. M.; Ataei, R.; Simon, A. F.
papers.abstract: Neuroligins are conserved postsynaptic adhesion proteins involved in synaptic function and behaviour. In Drosophila melanogaster, Neuroligin 3 (Nlg3) regulates social behaviour, sleep and synaptic architecture. We now report, through analysis of publicly available transcriptomics data, confirmed with RT-qPCR data, that loss-of-function of the nlg3 gene downregulates the expression of longevity-associated genes foxo, hsp70s, and hsp68. Graded genetic manipulation of the Drosophila melanogaster neuroligin 3 (nlg3) gene indeed modulates both social spacing and lifespan. Specifically, reduced nlg3 expression (via heterozygous deletion, or transposable-element insertion) extends lifespan in both sexes, while overexpression or complete deletion shortens it. In contrast, overexpression or complete loss of nlg3 leads the flies to be further apart (increased social distance, or social space), as does RNAi knockdown, while heterozygous reduction of nlg3 expression either lowers or does not alter the flies social space. This work identifies a previously unrecognized link between a conserved synaptic gene, social behaviour, and organismal longevity.

papers.title: Decoding lipid metabolic reprogramming in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: from tumor–microenvironment crosstalk to therapeutic resistance
papers.authors: Xingyu Liu; Zitong Ye; Liuyang Wang; Yubo Chi; Tongjia Chu; Ziyu Liu; Shanxiang Yu; Haocheng Yang; Xinyue Yin; Jian Zhang; Alfred Wei Chieh Kow; Huan Liu
papers.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is characterized by a nutrient-poor, hypoxic, and highly desmoplastic microenvironment that imposes substantial metabolic stress on malignant cells. Under these unfavorable conditions, lipid metabolism reprogramming provides cancer cells with the flexibility needed to maintain growth and survive therapeutic stress. Recent advances have uncovered new links between lipid metabolic reprogramming, the tumor microenvironment, and therapeutic resistance in PDAC, highlighting the need for an updated synthesis of this rapidly evolving field. In this review, we focus on the major tumor-intrinsic alterations in fatty acid and cholesterol–mevalonate metabolism, including changes in lipid synthesis, uptake, desaturation, storage, and oxidative utilization. These processes support membrane homeostasis, oncogenic signaling, and redox control, thereby linking lipid handling directly to tumor progression and treatment adaptation. We further review how these pathways are reshaped by the tumor microenvironment, where cancer-associated fibroblasts, immune cells, adipocytes, and neural-associated cells influence lipid availability, trafficking, and signaling. These reciprocal interactions can shape stromal plasticity, immune suppression, invasion, metastasis, and treatment response. We also evaluate current strategies targeting lipid metabolism and discuss why their clinical translation remains limited by metabolic compensation, tumor heterogeneity, drug specificity, and systemic toxicity. Overall, the available evidence suggests that lipid metabolism in PDAC is better understood as a dynamic, interconnected adaptive network rather than a set of isolated metabolic pathways. This perspective supports biomarker-guided combination strategies that target context-dependent lipid dependencies and treatment-induced metabolic adaptation, rather than relying on inhibition of a single pathway.

papers.title: Exploratory Untargeted Plasma Lipidomics Suggests Subtype-Associated Lipid Alterations in Hereditary Hemolytic Anemias
papers.authors: Neslihan Ayhan Donmez; Yesim Oztas; Tuba Reçber; Emirhan Nemutlu; Cagri Coskun; Sule Unal
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Hereditary hemolytic anemias (HHAs) are rare genetic disorders characterized by chronic hemolysis, systemic oxidative stress, and inflammation. Altered lipid homeostasis has previously been reported in HHAs; however, untargeted plasma lipidomic studies comparing HHA subtypes remain limited. This exploratory study aimed to characterize shared and subtype-specific plasma lipid alterations across five HHA subtypes. Methods: Forty-eight participants were enrolled, including 29 patients with HHA (6 with β-thalassemia, 5 with hereditary xerocytosis, 7 with hereditary spherocytosis, 5 with sickle cell disease, and 6 with congenital dyserythropoietic anemia) and 19 healthy controls. Plasma lipids were analyzed by untargeted liquid chromatography–quadrupole time-of-flight mass spectrometry, followed by multivariate, univariate, and lipid pathway analyses. Results: A total of 375 lipid species were putatively annotated, revealing both shared and putative subtype-specific lipid alterations across the five HHA subtypes. The putatively annotated species Cer 59:7;4O and PC 46:1 remained significantly altered after false discovery rate correction, whereas species such as PC 34:4 and Cer 42:3;2O showed only nominal subtype-specific differences. Mostly nominal alterations in individual ceramide, triglyceride, and phosphatidylcholine species were observed across most hemolytic groups relative to controls. Congenital dyserythropoietic anemia exhibited the fewest nominal differences from controls. Among the 25 species with nominal Kruskal–Wallis differences, SM 37:1;2O was the only lipid species that nominally differed from controls exclusively in this subtype. Conclusions: These exploratory, hypothesis-generating findings suggest that plasma lipidomics may help characterize lipid alterations accompanying chronic hemolysis. However, the candidate lipid species and predicted pathways require validation in larger, age-matched, independent cohorts.

papers.title: Incomplete Recovery of Cutaneous Lipid Homeostasis during Psoriasis Remission Links Mast Cell Activation to Relapse: A Mechanistic Study
papers.authors: Li Zhang; Ce Shuai; Han Cao; Lihong Chen; Jianglu Zhou; Feng Xue; Youcong Wang; Haoying Chen; Xia Li; Jie Zheng
papers.venue: International Journal of Dermatology and Venereology
papers.abstract: Objective: Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin disease characterized by relapse. Mast cells have been implicated in early relapse, but the mechanisms driving their activation remain unclear. Therefore, this study aimed to identify key regulatory factors associated with mast cell activation in psoriasis relapse. Methods: In this mechanistic study, longitudinal skin samples were collected from patients with psoriasis receiving IL-17A inhibitor therapy at Ruijin Hospital, between 2018 and 2020. Skin transcriptomes of psoriasis patients on IL-17A inhibitor therapy were compared at baseline, remission, and relapse between those with (n=6) or without (n=8) mast cell activation features. Mechanistic findings were validated in an imiquimod-induced psoriasiform mouse model using histopathology, transcriptomics, and metabolomic analyses. In addition, in vitro assays were performed to assess the effects of candidate mechanisms on mast cell function. Results: Bulk RNA-seq identified 102 differentially expressed genes during remission, including 93 downregulated genes predominantly enriched in lipid metabolism-related pathways. Compared with healthy controls, psoriasis-associated lipid metabolism genes remained incompletely restored during remission in patients with mast cell activation but normalized in patients without mast cell activation. Enrichment scores for lipid metabolism pathways were inversely correlated with mast cell activation signatures. In the murine model, restoration of skin lipid metabolism reduced mast cell retention including IL-17A + mast cells (8.33 ± 1.22 vs. 16.33 ± 1.15 per visual field, P = 0.008), and alleviated psoriasiform inflammation upon imiquimod re-challenge (51.82 ± 1.72 vs. 94.62 ± 5.59 μm, P vs. 16.56 ± 0.33%, P = 0.02) and reduced both IL-17A uptake (2.79 ± 0.40% vs 22.57 ± 0.20%, P vs. 720.6 ± 55.4 pg/mL, P = 0.02). Conclusion: Incomplete recovery of cutaneous lipid homeostasis during remission may sustain mast cell activation and contribute to psoriasis relapse. Restoration of skin barrier-associated lipid homeostasis, particularly ceramide metabolism, may represent a translational strategy to stabilize mast cells and delay disease recurrence.

papers.title: Lipid remodeling during phosphate starvation in plants: from metabolism to inter-organelle lipid transport.
papers.authors: Siqi Yan; Samia AlSayyad; Morgane Michaud
papers.abstract: Phosphate (Pi) starvation triggers extensive membrane lipid remodeling in plants, in which phospholipids are degraded and replaced by phosphorus-free glycolipids to recycle Pi while preserving membrane integrity. Although the metabolic pathways underlying this process have been extensively studied, the mechanisms coordinating lipid trafficking between organelles remain poorly understood. In this review, we summarize current knowledge of lipid metabolism during Pi starvation, including glycolipid synthesis, phospholipid and sphingolipid degradation, and triacylglycerol accumulation. We then discuss recent advances highlighting the emerging role of lipid transport in membrane remodeling. Finally, we highlight the major unanswered questions regarding the spatial organization of lipid remodeling and the molecular mechanisms linking lipid degradation, synthesis, and inter-organelle transport. Understanding these processes will be essential for building an integrated view of plant adaptation to phosphate limitation and for improving phosphorus-use efficiency in crops.

papers.title: Macrophage lipid signaling drives glioblastoma invasion and represents a therapeutic vulnerability.
papers.authors: Carla Pallarés-Moratalla; Mélanie Guyot; Krish Skandha Gopalan; Bernhard Robl; Jakub Idkowiak; Jonas Dehairs; Nina Ravoet; Tim F E Hendriks; Kinga Anna Nowak; Nikolina Dubroja Lakić; Linqian Weng; Vasileios Konstantakos; Xander Spotbeen; Lutgarde Serneels; Sarah-Maria Fendt; Stein Aerts; Frederik De Smet; Eva Cuypers; Johannes V Swinnen; Gabriele Bergers
papers.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is characterized by diffuse infiltration into the surrounding brain, limiting complete surgical resection, the strongest determinant of patient survival. The mechanisms driving this invasive growth remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify a lipid-mediated paracrine signaling axis through which tumor-associated microglia/macrophages promote glioma invasion. Integrating single-cell transcriptomics, spatial lipidomics, and functional perturbation across mouse models and human GBM samples, we show that invading tumor cells engage and reprogram myeloid cells via colony-stimulating factor-1 receptor (CSF1R)-PI3K signaling. This induces lipid metabolic reprogramming and secretion of bioactive lipids, including lysophosphatidylcholines (LPCs) and lysophosphatidic acids (LPAs), which promote GBM invasion through distinct downstream pathways. Disruption of this myeloid-GBM axis reduces lipid secretion and suppresses invasion. Targeting downstream LPA-LPA receptor (LPAR) or YAP/TAZ signaling further constrains invasion in a context-dependent manner. Together, these findings define a lipid-driven circuit linking the tumor microenvironment to glioma invasion and identify strategies to reduce infiltration and improve surgical resection.

papers.title: MiR-204-5p signalling modulates apoptosis and mitophagy-related changes after intracerebral hemorrhage in adult rats
papers.authors: Dongling Li; Xiaoqing Wen; wenqi Song; Yetong Ouyang; Qinghua Luo; Min Yin; Yuqin Zhong; Zhengfang Qin; Bing Bao; Xianming Cao; Moxin Wu; Zhiying Chen; Xiaoping Yin
papers.abstract: Abstract Background The survival of neurons around the hematoma is crucial for the recovery of neurological function after spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH). Neuronal apoptosis and mitochondrial quality control disturbances are important factors for secondary brain injury after ICH, but their molecular mechanisms have not been fully elucidated. This study investigated the role of miR-204-5p in ICH and analyzed its association with apoptotic and mitophagy-related signalling. Methods A collagenase-induced ICH model was established in adult male Sprague-Dawley rats. miR-204-5p expression was assessed in perihaematoma brain tissue and in serum from patients with ICH. Neurological deficits, brain water content and blood-brain barrier permeability were evaluated after intracerebroventricular administration of a miR-204-5p agomir. Apoptosis-associated markers and mitophagy-related proteins were assessed by western blotting, TUNEL staining, immunofluorescence and transmission electron microscopy. Target prediction, luciferase reporter assays and gene knockdown experiments were used to investigate TAOK1 and CAMK1. GATA3 promoter activity and the effects of donepezil pretreatment were also examined. Results miR-204-5p was reduced in perihaematoma brain tissue and in serum from patients with ICH, and lower serum levels were associated with higher NIHSS and mRS scores in the available clinical samples. miR-204-5p overexpression improved neurological deficits and reduced apoptosis-associated changes and mitophagy-related molecular and ultrastructural changes after ICH. TAOK1 and CAMK1 were identified as direct post-transcriptional targets of miR-204-5p by bioinformatic prediction, expression analysis and dual-luciferase assays. TAOK1 knockdown reduced TUNEL-positive signals, whereas CAMK1 knockdown attenuated mitochondrial ultrastructural abnormalities. GATA3 increased miR-204-5p promoter activity, and its expression was reduced after ICH. Donepezil pretreatment increased GATA3 expression and was associated with reduced apoptosis-associated and mitophagy-related changes. Conclusions Together, these findings suggest that the GATA3–miR-204-5p–CAMK1/TAOK1 axis may contribute to neuronal injury after ICH. Mitophagic flux and the causal relationships among these components remain to be established. The clinical association and donepezil findings are preliminary and require further validation.

papers.title: Mitochondrial transfer in cancer-immune crosstalk.
papers.authors: Yuhan Chen; Zhangui Tang; Jingyi Cheng
papers.venue: Biochimica et biophysica acta. Molecular basis of disease
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial transfer has emerged as a pivotal mechanism of intercellular metabolic reprogramming within the tumor microenvironment (TME), fundamentally reshaping cancer-immune crosstalk. This review provides a comprehensive synthesis of the regulatory triggers, molecular routes, and functional consequences of mitochondrial transfer in the tumor immune microenvironment. Mitochondrial exchange between tumor and immune cells occurs bidirectionally via tunneling nanotubes, extracellular vesicles, and other pathways, and is dynamically regulated by reactive oxygen species, inflammatory signaling, and metabolic stress. We delineate how this transfer exerts dual effects on antitumor immunity: tumor cells hijack functional mitochondria from T cells, macrophages, and stromal cells to fuel their proliferation and therapy resistance, while simultaneously delivering mutant mitochondria to immune cells to drive exhaustion and immune evasion. Conversely, artificial mitochondrial transfer to immune cells-including repolarization of tumor-associated macrophages via M1-derived mitochondria and metabolic augmentation of T cells and natural killer cells-demonstrates significant potential to reinvigorate antitumor immunity and overcome resistance to immune checkpoint blockade. We further discuss emerging strategies to block pro-tumoral mitochondrial hijacking through cytoskeletal inhibitors and extracellular vesicle modulators. Critical challenges for clinical translation-including precision delivery, sustained functional integration, mitochondrial DNA heteroplasmy risks, and interactions with conventional therapies-are also addressed. By integrating mechanistic insights with therapeutic innovation, this review positions mitochondrial transfer as both a targetable driver of immunosuppression and a platform for next-generation cancer immunotherapies.

papers.title: Neuroinflammation in levodopa-induced dyskinesia in Parkinson's disease: current state of the art.
papers.authors: Bruno Lopes Santos-Lobato; Tatiane Piedade de Souza Machado; Luiz Vinicius Silva Correa; Margarete Zanardo Gomes; Elaine A Del-Bel; Vitor Tumas
papers.abstract: Levodopa-induced dyskinesia (LID) remains a major limitation of long-term dopaminergic therapy in Parkinson's disease (PD). Although LID is classically attributed to maladaptive corticostriatal plasticity driven by pulsatile dopaminergic stimulation in the dopamine-denervated striatum, accumulating evidence indicates that chronic neuroinflammation may lower the threshold for LID development and expression. Here, we synthesize preclinical, human biomarkers, neuroimaging, and genetic findings that support neuroinflammation as a mechanistic bridge between cellular stress and circuit-level maladaptation. In animal models, pharmacological modulation of inflammation-linked pathways, particularly nitrergic signaling, antibiotic repurposing, and cannabinoid-based strategies, attenuates abnormal involuntary movements and reduces striatal glial reactivity, implicating an inflammation-plasticity coupling in LID. In humans, post-mortem studies implicate regionally constrained mitochondrial DNA abnormalities and lipid dysregulation in the striatum, while biofluid metabolomics supports altered nitric oxide generation and lipid pathways associated with LID severity. Neuroimaging studies reveal markers consistent with oxidative stress and neurovascular dysfunction, and genetic studies link LID risk to variants in genes involved in lysosomal function, mitochondrial homeostasis, and inflammatory transcriptional programs. Integrated with the classic mechanisms of LID pathophysiology, we propose a conceptual model organized around three interrelated dimensions: (i) the topographical distribution of neuroinflammatory changes, particularly within the striatum; (ii) the interaction of neuroinflammation with mitochondrial dysfunction and lipid dysregulation; and (iii) the modifying influence of genetic susceptibility. This model motivates biomarker-guided, randomized trials targeting specific inflammatory nodes to prevent or mitigate LID.

papers.title: SYNJ2BP is associated with mitochondrial abnormalities and skeletal muscle atrophy in experimental models
papers.authors: Jian Zhang; Yuxia Yang; Xiangji Meng; XiaoFei Wang; Jihang Dai; Pei Zhang; Jingcheng Wang; Wenyong Fei
papers.venue: Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology
papers.abstract: Skeletal muscle atrophy is associated with mitochondrial dysfunction, but the contribution of synaptojanin 2 binding protein (SYNJ2BP) remains unclear. Proteomic profiling of human supraspinatus muscle identified increased SYNJ2BP abundance in atrophied tissue, together with changes in mitochondrial and calcium-related protein sets. Increased SYNJ2BP abundance was also observed in mouse supraspinatus muscle after tendon transection. In C2C12 cells, SYNJ2BP overexpression was accompanied by altered myogenic and atrophy-associated proteins, abnormal mitochondrial ultrastructure, lower ATP content, and increased Rhod-2 fluorescence. VBIT-4 attenuated several of these changes but also reduced SYNJ2BP abundance, limiting interpretation as a selective downstream rescue. SYNJ2BP, IP3R1, and GRP75 were recovered in VDAC1 immunoprecipitates. Increased VDAC1 bait recovery and differences in input abundance preclude interpreting greater protein recovery as stronger relative association. In a separate mouse hindlimb immobilization model, local SYNJ2BP knockdown was associated with preserved mitochondrial morphology, less muscle wasting, and improved physical performance. These complementary observations implicate SYNJ2BP in muscle wasting and motivate investigation of IP3R1/GRP75/VDAC1-associated calcium regulation. They do not establish a shared causal mechanism across models. The GFP-containing expression vector also necessitates independent validation of the reactive oxygen species and membrane-potential measurements. Further work should establish physiological expression relevance, cell differentiation status, and the direction and specificity of calcium transfer.

papers.title: Drp1-mediated mitochondrial fission contributes to ox-LDL-induced phenotypic transition and calcification in human coronary artery smooth muscle cells.
papers.authors: Zhi-Bo Fu; Yu Li; Shu-Ying Ding; Jun-Yi Luo; Xiang Ma; Zi-Xiang Yu
papers.abstract: Vascular smooth muscle cell (VSMC) phenotypic transition is central to vascular calcification (VC), a major complication of cardiovascular disease. To investigate how oxidized low-density lipoprotein (ox-LDL) drives VSMC reprogramming, we examined dynamin-related protein 1 (Drp1) in human coronary artery smooth muscle cells (HCASMCs). Three experimental series were used. Pharmacological series: control, ox-LDL, ox-LDL + Mdivi-1, ox-LDL + p38 inhibitor, and osteogenic medium as positive control. Genetic series: ox-LDL + si-NC and ox-LDL + si-Drp1. Epistasis series: si-NC, si-NC + ox-LDL, si-Drp1 + ox-LDL, and si-Drp1 + ox-LDL + anisomycin. Exposure to 25 μg/mL ox-LDL for 18 days induced phenotypic changes and calcification, with increased mineralization markers and Drp1 expression accompanied by mitochondrial fission. Runx2 was elevated, whereas SM22α and α-SMA were reduced, indicating an osteogenic shift. Drp1 inhibition attenuated mitochondrial fragmentation, phenotypic conversion, and calcification, with partial restoration of mitochondrial membrane potential (red/green ratio). p38 MAPK inhibition similarly alleviated phenotypic transition and calcification, downregulated Fis1, increased SM22α and α-SMA, and reduced Runx2. In epistasis experiments, p38 reactivation largely reversed the protective effects of Drp1 knockdown, suggesting that the effects of Drp1-dependent mitochondrial fission are mediated, at least in part, through the p38 MAPK signaling pathway, with Fis1 as a candidate further downstream node. Thus, Drp1-dependent mitochondrial fission and the p38 MAPK signaling pathway it engages are candidate entry points for further investigation in VC; in vivo validation remains necessary.

papers.title: Excessive mitochondrial fission in myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury: Pathophysiological relevance and potential cardioprotective modulation by plant-derived interventions and electroacupuncture
papers.authors: Li Sun; Xing-Yi Sun; Zi-Han Na; Yi-Jia Liu; Lin Li; Tian-Yu Cao; Xin-Ran Li; Ya-Dong Fan; Gui-Ping Hu; Shuo Wang
papers.abstract: Myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury (MI/RI) remains an unresolved problem despite reperfusion therapies, including percutaneous coronary intervention. Mitochondria are central mediators of reperfusion-associated cardiomyocyte injury, with excessive fission implicated as a potentially important mechanism linking acute metabolic stress to fragmentation, bioenergetic failure, and cell death. Reactive oxygen species, Ca2+ overload, mitochondrial permeability transition pore opening and membrane-potential loss promote dynamin-related protein 1-centered (Drp1-centered) fission, often involving mitochondrial fission factor, mitochondrial fission 1 protein and site-specific Drp1 phosphorylation. By disrupting mitochondrial networks and oxidative phosphorylation, this process contributes to cytochrome c release, apoptosis, microvascular dysfunction and impaired recovery. Impaired mitofusin 1/2-mediated and optic atrophy 1-mediated fusion limits repair and quality control, supporting investigation of this fission-dominant imbalance as a target for cardioprotection. Preclinical studies suggest plant-derived natural products, multi-component botanical preparations and electroacupuncture may influence this imbalance. Reported effects include attenuated Drp1 signaling, altered fusion-protein expression, preserved membrane potential, inhibited permeability transition, reduced oxidative stress and apoptosis, and modulated upstream metabolic/stress-responsive pathways. However, hypoxia/reoxygenation, oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation, non-reperfused ischemia/infarction and stress models provide surrogate or supportive evidence rather than direct evidence of MI/RI. Heterogeneity in models, timing, dosage, readouts, causal validation and botanical quality control limits interpretation. This review examines these mechanisms, interventions and translational priorities. Clinical efficacy and safety of these interventions in MI/RI have not been established.

papers.title: Magnolol alleviates high-fat diet-induced steatosis, inflammation and fibrosis in obesity-associated liver injuries via MOGAT1-mediated lipid metabolism and NF-κB signaling
papers.authors: Ziqing Huang; Zixia Huang; Linfei Luo; Zhengqiang Wu; Zhili Wen; Zhihua Xiao
papers.abstract: Background Magnolol (MAG), a bioactive compound from Magnolia officinalis, possesses anti-inflammatory and lipid-lowering properties, but its role in obesity-associated liver injury and its molecular targets remain unknown. Methods High-fat diet (HFD)-fed mice were treated with MAG (10 or 20 mg/kg) daily for 7 days. AML12 hepatocytes were challenged with PA with or without MAG pretreatment. Liver injury was evaluated by histology, serum biochemistry, qPCR and Western blot. RNA-seq and mechanistic studies were performed to identify MAG-regulated pathways and targets. Results MAG significantly reduced hepatic lipid accumulation, serum transaminases, and collagen deposition in HFD-fed mice. RNA-seq identified monoacylglycerol O-acyltransferase 1 (MOGAT1) as the most significantly downregulated lipogenic gene by MAG. MOGAT1 expression correlated positively with liver triglyceride and injury markers. MAG also suppressed HFD-induced NF-κB activation (reduced P65 phosphorylation and nuclear translocation, lower IL-6, TNF-α, IL-1β). These findings were recapitulated in PA-treated AML12 cells. Critically, MOGAT1 overexpression largely reversed MAG-mediated suppression of inflammatory and fibrotic responses, demonstrating a causal role of MOGAT1 in MAG’s protective effects. Conclusion MAG alleviates HFD-induced hepatic steatosis, inflammation and fibrogenic responses by suppressing MOGAT1-mediated triglyceride synthesis and subsequent NF-κB-driven inflammation. This study identifies MOGAT1 as a novel downstream effector and functional mediator of MAG, providing new mechanistic insight into its hepatoprotective action and supporting its therapeutic potential for obesity-associated liver injuries.

papers.title: Multifaceted Physiological Roles of Lipoproteins and Understanding Atherosclerosis: Crosstalk Between Lipoproteins and Bioactive Lipids.
papers.authors: Makoto Kurano
papers.abstract: Traditional management of atherosclerosis focuses primarily on cholesterol and triglycerides; however, lipoproteins also transport bioactive lipids that critically regulate systemic inflammation and metabolic health. This review highlights the diverse physiological and clinical roles of apolipoproteins and bioactive lipids beyond classical lipid accumulation. First, we discuss how hepatic transporters NPC1L1 and ABCG5/8 modulate glucose metabolism and handle non-cholesterol lipids, including phytosterols. Second, we emphasize the apolipoprotein M (ApoM) and sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P) axis. ApoM protects S1P from degradation and directly mediates the pleiotropic benefits of high-density lipoprotein (HDL), including anti-apoptotic, antithrombotic, and renoprotective effects. Third, reverse translational research utilizing genome-wide association studies identifies apolipoprotein D (ApoD) as a key anti-inflammatory modulator. Finally, clinical lipidomics underscores the importance of "minor" lysophospholipids, such as lysophosphatidylinositol and lysophosphatidylserine, alongside lysophosphatidic acid in the pathogenesis of acute coronary syndrome. Understanding the dynamic crosstalk between lipid transporters, apolipoproteins, and bioactive lipids provides novel mechanistic insights into cardiovascular and metabolic diseases, paving the way for innovative biomarkers and precision therapeutic strategies.

papers.title: Randomized comparative blood glucose, lipids, malondialdehyde, liver enzymes, and C-reactive protein responses to laser acupuncture versus interscapular wet cupping in fatty liver
papers.authors: Ali Ismail; Yousef M. Alshehre; Ahmed Mohamed Abdelhalim Elfahl; Ahmed Bayuomy Abo Elatta; Ahmed M. Elfahl; Sami Kamal Mohamed Elgendy
papers.abstract: Background: Wide appreciation of the use of complementary therapies is reported by patients with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). Objectives: This study aimed to compare the effect of interscapular wet cupping (IWC) versus laser acupuncture (LA) on systolic and diastolic blood pressure, aspartate transaminase, pulse rate, alanine transaminase, serum malondialdehyde, fasting blood glucose, serum high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP), and blood lipids (total cholesterol, triglycerides, low-density lipoprotein, high-density lipoprotein) in NAFLD patients. This was a randomized comparative study. Materials and methods: Sixty fatty liver participants were recruited from the Internal Diseases Outpatient Clinic, Specialized Clinics, Badr City, Egypt. Patients were randomly assigned to the IWC or LA group. For 3 months, the TWC group received 2 cupping sessions per month (on days 0 and 14). The selected acupoints received 3 LA sessions per week for 3 months. We assessed the above measurements before and after the 3-month complementaryinterventional study period. Results: Significant improvements were reported in the IWC and LA groups (except for serum hs-CRP in the IWC group). Conclusion: LA or IWC may help in controlling blood pressure, blood glucose, lipids, inflammatory markers, liver enzymes, and oxidative stress markers in patients with fatty liver.

papers.title: Recent advances in understanding the regulatory mechanisms of P4-ATPase lipid flippases.
papers.authors: Pauline Funke; Mathilde Roth; Thibaud Dieudonné; Guillaume Lenoir
papers.abstract: P4-ATPases establish and maintain transbilayer lipid asymmetry in eukaryotic membranes by transporting phospholipids from the exoplasmic to the cytosolic membrane leaflet at the expense of ATP hydrolysis. In recent years, biochemical analysis together with an increasing number of cryo-electron microscopy structures has substantially increased our understanding of the lipid transport cycle and substrate recognition by P4-ATPases. However, the underlying molecular mechanism governing P4-ATPase activation and regulation remains less well understood. The present review aims to summarize current insights into the molecular mechanisms controlling P4-ATPase activation and regulation. We discuss autoinhibition by N- and C-terminal extensions, activation by regulatory lipids, particularly phosphoinositides, regulation by interacting proteins including small GTPases and guanine nucleotide exchange factors, and post-translational modifications, especially phosphorylation. Together, these studies reveal that P4-ATPase activity is controlled by a complex and multilayered regulatory network that enables precise control of lipid transport. Future studies combining structural, biochemical, and cellular approaches will be essential to elucidate how these mechanisms cooperate to maintain membrane lipid homeostasis and support diverse cellular functions.

papers.title: SenescenceBioKG reveals full-text-supported biomaterial design, mechanisms, and regeneration patterns in senescence-oriented tissue engineering
papers.authors: Shengyue Li; Xinxin Jing; Jin Tan; Qiang Zhang
papers.abstract: Background Senescence-oriented biomaterial studies provide evidence regarding material design, responsive behavior, cellular targets, mechanisms, regeneration, and validation across different full-text sections. However, publication-level labels cannot reliably answer questions that require several of these relations to occur in the same study. Methods We constructed SenescenceBioKG based on 283 original experimental or translational full-text studies. Candidate relations were generated under a typed ontology, adjudicated against same-record evidence, linked to unique evidence identifiers, and canonicalized into a queryable graph. Fifteen competency questions were evaluated using graph traversal and an independently implemented dataframe method. A local read-only R Shiny Explorer was developed for evidence inspection. Results The frozen graph contained 654 canonical nodes, 1,868 supported edges, and 1,868 linked evidence records. Within the curated corpus, strict material responsiveness comprised 64 RESPONDS TO edges from 55 studies and 55 material platforms, led by acidic pH and reactive oxygen species. Same-study analyses recovered responsive-design modules and 35 complete target-cell–mechanism–regeneration modules. Mesenchymal stem/stromal cells, senescent cells, and macrophage or innate immune populations were recurrent targets, whereas oxidative-stress control, mitochondrial homeostasis, and NF-κB/Senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) signaling frequently accompanied bone, wound/skin, cartilage, and disc endpoints. Validation was concentrated in Cell and Small-Animal studies; Organoid/chip and Large-Animal evidence was sparse, and no Clinical edge was supported. All 15 queries achieved exact-set agreement between the two implementations, with macro precision, recall, and F1 values of 1.00. Conclusion SenescenceBioKG provides a full-text-supported structure for examining smart and responsive biomaterial design, fabrication, cellular evidence, regenerative outcomes, and validation gaps. Its provenance model separates co-supported evidence from causal inference and supports reproducible, material-centered retrieval.

papers.title: Single-Cell Transcriptomic and Regulatory Network Analyses Identify a Putative HNF4A–OXR1 Association Linked to Podocyte Mitochondrial Dysfunction in Diabetic Kidney Disease
papers.authors: Zhenkun Yang; Shimin Jiang; Wen Cui; Jiahui Zhou; Wenge Li
papers.abstract: Podocyte injury is a central pathological event in diabetic kidney disease (DKD), but the mitochondrial regulatory mechanisms underlying podocyte dysfunction remain incompletely defined. We integrated single-nucleus RNA-seq data from human renal biopsies in GSE195460 with podocyte-specific differential expression, functional enrichment, mitochondrial gene annotation, co-expression network analysis, machine learning feature selection, pseudotime analysis, in silico knockout, transcription factor enrichment, motif analysis, and molecular docking; findings were externally evaluated in GSE209781. Podocytes showed prominent disease-associated transcriptomic perturbation, with 677 exploratory cell-level differentially expressed genes and enrichment of cytoskeletal, adhesion, developmental, oxidative phosphorylation, and metabolic pathways. Thirty-one mitochondrial-related differentially expressed genes were identified, and OXR1 was prioritized as a candidate regulatory hub based on consistent downregulation, network centrality, machine learning selection, and external validation. HNF4A was predicted as an upstream regulator linked to OXR1 and other mitochondrial targets. In silico OXR1 perturbation increased the predicted injured-state probability from 15% to 82%, while promoter motif analysis provided additional computational support for a putative HNF4A–OXR1 regulatory relationship. These findings highlight OXR1 as a candidate associated with podocyte mitochondrial dysfunction in DKD and suggest a putative HNF4A–OXR1 regulatory relationship.

papers.title: Targeting taurine metabolism improves mitochondrial function in mt-tRNA mutation-associated mitochondrial disease
papers.authors: Xingyu Zhuang; Ying Zhao; Jianing Wang; Yan Lin; Jiayin Wang; Weiyue Si; Chuanzhu Yan; Busu Li; Kunqian Ji
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Mitochondrial diseases caused by mt-tRNA mutations disrupt oxidative phosphorylation and metabolic homeostasis, but effective treatment options remain scarce. Given the central role of nutrient metabolism in mitochondrial function, we investigated whether metabolite disturbances could reveal actionable therapeutic targets. Methods We conducted integrated transcriptomic and targeted metabolomic analyses in patients with mt-tRNA mutation-related mitochondrial disease, using skeletal muscle biopsies for transcriptome profiling and serum samples for metabolite assessment. The functional relevance of the identified metabolic alteration was tested in mutant cells following taurine supplementation. Results Transcriptomic analysis revealed coordinated upregulation of mitochondrial-encoded respiratory chain genes and downregulation of nuclear-encoded oxidative phosphorylation subunits, consistent with mito-nuclear transcriptional decoupling. Targeted serum metabolomics demonstrated a 26% reduction in taurine, accompanied by increased expression of genes involved in taurine biosynthesis and transport, suggesting a compensatory adaptation to systemic taurine deficiency. Importantly, taurine supplementation improved mitochondrial respiration, restored membrane potential, increased mtDNA content, and attenuated reactive oxygen species accumulation in mutant cells. Conclusions Our findings identify an association between altered taurine homeostasis and mt-tRNA mutation-associated mitochondrial dysfunction and provide in vitro evidence that taurine can modify selected mitochondrial parameters in an mt-tRNA mutation fibroblast model. These results provide a mechanistic rationale for future clinical studies targeting taurine metabolism in mitochondrial disorders.

papers.title: Integrating tissue proteomics and bioactive lipid analysis of ovine tissue samples identifies functional relations of bioactive lipids
papers.authors: Gerhard Hagn; Florien Jenner; Andrea Bileck; Sinan Gültekin; Mats Hamberg; Thomas Mohr; Christopher Gerner; Iris Gerner
papers.abstract: Bioactive lipids are potent effector molecules that may help to reveal specific information about biological processes. However, analytical challenges and incomplete functional annotations remain as obstacles. We hypothesized that the functional annotation of these lipids may be improved by projecting enriched Gene Ontology (GO) terms derived from proteomics to correlating bioactive lipids. To that aim, thirteen organs and tissues from sheep ( Ovis aries ) were analyzed using mass spectrometry-based untargeted proteomics and bioactive lipid analysis. In total, 4717 proteins and 168 bioactive lipids, including fatty acids and their conjugates, oxylipins (octadecanoids, eicosanoids, and docosanoids), lyso-phosphatidylcholines (LPCs) and lyso-phosphatidylethanolamines (LPEs), endocannabinoids and related fatty amides, and bile acids and related sterol lipids were determined. Thereof, the correct identification of 114 lipids was confirmed using commercially available analytical standards, whereas the identity of the previously uncharacterized oxylipin 4-hydroxy-eicosatetraenoic acid (4-HETE) was verified through in-house chemical synthesis. Co-expression and clustering analyses are consistent with our hypothesis via independently corroborating known bioactive lipid functions and suggested novel functional relations. Amongst other observations, 18-HETE and 19-HETE were related to mitochondrial fatty acid beta-oxidation, 11,12-dihydroxy-eicosatetraenoic acid (DiHETE), 15-deoxy-prostaglandin J2 and 5(6)-epoxy-eicosatrienoic acid (EET) were related to chemical synaptic transmission, arachidonoyl ethanolamide phosphate was related to muscle contraction and numerous LPCs and LPEs were related to exosome formation. Tissue levels of polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs), pro-resolving mediators and the newly characterized 4-HETE were related to the cellular protein synthesis and folding machinery. The latter finding suggested that PUFAs and their derivatives support protein synthesis fidelity in addition to efferocytosis, both essential contributors for the effective resolution of inflammation.

papers.title: Profiling Temperature-Dependent Lipid Remodeling in Yersinia pestis Using Ion Mobility-Mass Spectrometry and Ozonolysis
papers.authors: Dylan H. Ross; Joshua R. Hansen; Meagan C. Burnet; Josie G. Eder; Brooke L. Deatherage Kaiser; Xueyun Zheng
papers.venue: Journal of the American Society for Mass Spectrometry
papers.abstract: Abstract Yersinia pestisundergoes dramatic physiological changes as it transitions from its flea vector (∼20–30 °C) to mammalian hosts (37 °C), including remodeling of its cell envelope lipids to evade innate immunity and enhance virulence. While various temperature-dependent changes in this organism have been previously documented, the broader lipidome remains poorly characterized. We applied liquid chromatography coupled with ion mobility spectrometry and tandem mass spectrometry (LC-IMS-MS/MS), in addition to ozone-induced dissociation (OzID), to comprehensively profile lipids in three attenuated Y. pestis strains (A1122, KIM D27, and KIM D1) grown at 30 and 37 °C. Untargeted lipidomic analysis identified 97 lipids across multiple classes, with principal component analysis revealing temperature-dependent clustering patterns distinct from strain-specific variations. Comparison of lipid profiles between temperatures revealed many significantly differentially expressed lipids per strain, with most strain-specific responses rather than shared across all strains. OzID fragmentation successfully identified double-bond positions for common unsaturated fatty acids and lysophospholipids, also enabling structural discrimination between monounsaturated and cyclopropyl fatty acid isomers. Notably, lipids containing cyclopropyl fatty acids were significantly upregulated at 37 °C across all three strains, suggesting a conserved temperature-responsive mechanism for enhancing membrane stability during mammalian host infection. Our study demonstrates that comprehensive, high-detailed, structurally resolved lipidomics reveals temperature-dependent lipid remodeling characteristics in Y. pestis that may support host transition and virulence, with potential applications for identifying lipid biomarkers.

papers.title: Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) mediated gut breast crosstalk in breast cancer: integrative network analysis of molecular signaling, immune infiltration and prognostic biomarkers
papers.authors: Tariq Aziz; Layla A. Alahmari; Nawal H. Siddig; Mai M. Almsaud; Fahad Al-Asmari; Huda A. Alqahtani; Rasha Alonaizan; Yolande Sandrine Mengue Ngadena
papers.abstract: Introduction Breast cancer is a heterogeneous malignancy in which metabolic dysregulation, immune remodelling, and complex host microbiota interactions contribute to disease progression and therapeutic response. Emerging evidence suggests that gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), including acetate, propionate, and butyrate, may act as important molecular mediators linking the gut microbiome to systemic immune and tumor-associated signalling. However, the molecular networks through which SCFA-mediated signalling may influence breast cancer progression and the tumor immune microenvironment remains poorly characterized. This study aimed to investigate the potential regulatory mechanisms underlying the gut-breast axis by integrating SCFA host interaction networks in breast cancer transcriptomic, prognostic, immune infiltration, and drug gene interaction analyses. Methods The SCFA-host interactome was constructed from the combination of HMDB and PubChem data in a protein-protein interaction network. The identification of hub genes was conducted through topological analysis, followed by validation using TCGA-BRCA RNA-seq data, Kaplan-Meier Survival Analysis, TIMER2.0 immune analysis, and DGIdb repurposing analysis. Results The findings indicated that the genes STAT3, HIF1A, and IL6 served as key nodes connecting SCFA signalling and cancer formation. Selected SCFAs, such as propionate, have direct experimental evidence of involvement in the modulation of the JAK2/STAT3 pathway in breast cancer models, while butyrate has been associated with several breast cancer-related signalling and epigenetic mechanisms. Associations were most strongly identified in acetate which was mainly related to metabolic and immune regulatory pathways. This computational analysis did not give a quantitative ranking of the strength of interaction between SCFA and hub genes. In exploratory survival analysis without multiple-testing correction, increased STAT3 and HIF1A expression was associated with unfavourable relapse-free survival. SCFA-associated immune targets showed positive correlations with CD8+ T-cell infiltration. Discussion This study identifies the SCFA-host interactome as an essential regulatory network in breast cancer. Uncovering metabolic and signalling chokepoints such as STAT3 leads to the discovery of new biomarkers for prognosis and drug targets. This highlights the possibility of exploiting the gut-breast axis to increase immune cell penetration.

papers.title: Transcriptomics Reveals Mesenchymal Stem Cell-Derived Exosomes Activate Hepatocyte Longevity-Regulating Pathway in Acute-On-Chronic Liver Failure
papers.authors: Deng-na Lin; Yong-qi Zhang; Hai-xia Sun; Yang Li; Wen-yu Li; Jing Zhang; Xiao-hua Yang; Xiang Gao
papers.abstract: Background: Acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF), a rapidly progressive condition with high short-term mortality in patients with chronic liver disease, has shown therapeutic responsiveness to mesenchymal stem cell-derived exosomes (MSC-exos) in preclinical studies, where exosome administration significantly attenuates hepatic injury. To comprehensively delineate the mechanistic basis of this therapeutic effect, we conducted integrated miRNA and mRNA sequencing analyses on liver tissues obtained from exosome-treated ACLF murine models. Methods: Mice subjected to a CCl4-based acute-on-chronic liver injury regimen received saline or an MSC-derived extracellular vesicle (EV) preparation intravenously through the tail vein. Liver miRNA and mRNA profiles were examined by differential expression, GSEA, functional enrichment, exploratory LASSO feature selection and integrative network analysis. Expression measurements were complemented by senescence-associated transcript assays, a Cat 3′UTR reporter assay and CCK-8 assessment in cell models. Results: Exosome treatment significantly activated longevity-regulating pathways, mitophagy, and glutathione metabolism in ACLF mice, concurrent with characteristic remodeling of hepatic immune infiltration involving follicular helper T cells, activated NK cells, and macrophage subpopulations. Hepatic injury severity demonstrated positive correlations with mmu-let-7j and Mmp27, and negative associations with mmu-let-7f-2-3p and Tmem8b. The reconstructed miRNA-mRNA network converged on FoxO signaling-mediated regulation of oxidative stress, cellular senescence and autophagy, with FoxO/Catalase (Cat) identified as core regulators. Experimental studies confirmed that MSC-derived exosomes downregulated miR-7b-5p in hepatocytes and enhanced Cat expression, with attenuation of cellular senescence. Conclusions: Integrative transcriptomic analysis revealed that MSC-exos activate the FoxO/Cat axis through miRNA-mRNA interactome remodeling, thereby orchestrating coordinated antioxidant, pro-autophagic, and anti-senescence effects alongside immune microenvironment reprogramming in liver failure. These findings establish a pivotal theoretical framework for developing exosome-based therapeutic strategies targeting hepatic disorders.

papers.title: Histone Modifications at the Intersection of Aging, Neuroinflammation and Metabolism in Alzheimer's Disease.
papers.authors: Liang J, Cao H, Ren X, Sha N, Han X, Jiang L, Liu B, Zhao W.
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Aging, neuroinflammation and metabolic dysfunction are tightly intertwined in Alzheimer's disease (AD), but how transient pathological signals become persistent cellular states remains poorly understood. Histone post‐translational modifications (PTMs) provide a dynamic interface between extracellular stimuli, cellular metabolism and chromatin state. This Review examines how canonical histone modifications and emerging metabolite‐derived acylations regulate inflammatory and stress‐responsive programmes across microglia, astrocytes and neurons during aging and AD. We discuss how amyloid‐β, tau pathology, metabolic dysfunction and innate immune signaling converge on histone‐modifying machinery, and how reciprocal interactions between metabolism and chromatin may stabilize disease‐associated cell states. Particular attention is given to cellular senescence and neuroimmune memory, while emphasizing the context dependence of individual histone marks across cell types, genomic regions and disease stages. We further evaluate evidence for causality using three criteria: perturbation, persistence and reversibility. This framework distinguishes chromatin states that accompany ongoing pathology from those capable of sustaining pathological cell states beyond their initiating signals. Finally, we consider therapeutic strategies targeting histone‐modifying enzymes, chromatin readers and metabolic inputs to restore chromatin plasticity and promote resolution of chronic neuroinflammation.

papers.title: Aging remodels progenitor and niche interactions in lung regeneration
papers.authors: Fernanda Toscano-Marquez; Angeles Garcia-Vicente; Uriel Camacho-Silverio; Tania Valdivia-Herrera; Mariana Río de la Loza; Elisa Hernández-Xóchihua; Remedios Ramírez; Moises Selman; Annie Pardo; Yair Romero
papers.abstract: Introduction Progenitor cells in aged tissues undergo changes in their microenvironment that may impact their functionality during regeneration. Despite recent advances in understanding the role of adult lung progenitors, the impact of aging on these cells remains unclear. Methods To analyze aging modifications, we used aged wild-type mice of 18–24 months old, and Zmpste24 –/– deficient mice, which exhibit an accelerated phenotype. A three-dimensional organoid culture system was employed to assess in vitro regenerative capacity. Additionally, cells were isolated and characterized with senescence and autophagy markers. Results Our findings revealed that lung epithelial cells from aged mice and Zmpste24 –/– mice retain organoid forming potential, maintaining their phenotype and cellular homeostasis through increased autophagy-associated transcriptional response, particularly when co-cultured with young fibroblasts. Moreover, these progenitor cells may exhibit increased susceptibility to mechanical stress with aging potentially associated with reduced nuclear lamins and the Zmpste24 defect. This vulnerability is illustrated by FACS sorting, which can further compromise their regenerative potential. By contrast, cultured fibroblasts from Zmpste24 –/– mice show nuclear defects and acquire a senescent phenotype, characterized by the mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) activation and reduced autophagy, which in turn impairs organoid formation. Discussion Our results indicate that, in aging, progenitor cells and their fibroblast niche integrate microenvironmental signals that shape cell-cell interactions essential for lung regeneration.

papers.title: Cell-Free Hemoglobin Drives CD163+ Macrophage Reprogramming and Drp1-Dependent Mitochondrial Transfer to Promote Septic Cardiac Dysfunction
papers.authors: Yuzhou Xiao; Yingjiao Liao; Yifei Liu; Guanglin Peng; Yinrui Ma; Qianyi Zeng; Ke Sun; Gautam Sethi; Ruijun Tang; He Huang; Rui Song; Bing Chen; Chenyang Duan
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Severe trauma is commonly accompanied by secondary infection and multiple organ dysfunction, wherein sepsis and SIMD constitute predominant determinants of fatal outcomes. Despite this, the mechanistic connection between systemic hemolysis and cardiac immune remodeling has yet to be defined. Accordingly, this study was designed to determine whether CFH drives septic cardiac injury and to elucidate the cellular and molecular basis underlying this process. Methods Clinical samples from patients with sepsis, cecal ligation and puncture (CLP) mouse models, single-cell RNA sequencing, metabolomic profiling, high-resolution live-cell imaging, and genetic manipulation were integrated to characterize CFH-mediated cardiac remodeling. Intercellular mitochondrial transfer was dynamically tracked using fluorescence imaging and super-resolution microscopy. A hemoglobin-targeting nanoparticle (HbAb-NP) was developed to evaluate the therapeutic potential of CFH scavenging. Results Circulating CFH was markedly elevated in septic patients and CLP mice and was associated with myocardial hemoglobin deposition, endothelial barrier disruption, cardiac dysfunction, and poor survival. CFH exposure was associated with an increased relative proportion of a metabolically reprogrammed CD163+ macrophage subset through activation of the glycolysis–NF-κB1 signaling axis. These macrophages exhibited mitochondrial dysfunction and transferred damaged mitochondria to endothelial cells via tunneling nanotubes (TNTs), resulting in oxidative stress, impaired mitochondrial respiration, endothelial barrier disruption, and reduced angiogenic capacity. Mechanistically, Drp1 facilitated TNT formation by activating the Cdc42/Rac1–cofilin/profilin pathway to drive actin cytoskeletal remodeling. Therapeutically, HbAb-NP efficiently scavenged circulating CFH, suppressed CD163+ macrophage activation, alleviated endothelial injury, improved cardiac function, and prolonged survival in septic mice. Conclusions This study identifies circulating CFH as a previously unrecognized upstream regulator linking systemic hemolysis to cardiac immune microenvironment remodeling during sepsis. CFH-induced CD163+ macrophage reprogramming and Drp1-dependent pathological mitochondrial transfer establish a macrophage–mitochondria–endothelial injury axis that drives SIMD. Targeting circulating CFH represents a promising therapeutic strategy for sepsis-associated cardiac dysfunction.

papers.title: Combined supplementation effects of bacterial organic selenium and vitamin E on post-mortem meat quality, selenium bioaccumulation, serum lipid metabolism and selenoprotein expression in spent laying hens
papers.authors: Nurafiqah Najwa Zainudin; Aliyu Ibrahim Muhammad; Nazri Nayan; Anjas Asmara Samsudin
papers.abstract: Context Antioxidants from biological sources play a vital role in preventing oxidative cellular damage in livestock. The dietary inclusion of biogenic organic selenium produced by Stenotrophomonas maltophilia (ADS18) represents a novel antioxidant strategy in poultry nutrition. Aim This study investigated the effects of combined dietary supplementation of diverse selenium (Se) sources and vitamin E on tissue Se deposition, systemic lipid profiles, antioxidant capacity, and postmortem muscle quality attributes in spent laying hens. Method One hundred and twenty 68-week-old Lohman Brown-Classic spent hens were randomly assigned to the following four dietary treatments for 90 days: a basal control (T1), basal diet supplemented with 250 mg/kg vitamin E and 0.3 mg/kg Se as sodium selenite (T2), selenium yeast (T3), or biogenic bacterial selenium (ADS18; T4). Key results Muscle Se deposition significantly higher in hens receiving Se sources (ADS18 and Se-yeast) than in inorganic Se and control groups. Co-supplementation of ADS18 and vitamin E significantly improved systemic lipid profile, characterised by increased high-density lipoprotein (HDL) and reduced triglyceride and low-density lipoprotein (LDL) concentrations. At the molecular level, organic Se combined with vitamin E significantly upregulated SELW1 and GPX4 mRNA expression. SELW1 expression was strongly associated with Se influx, serving as a responsive biomarker of bioavailability, whereas GPX4 remained stable across treatments. However, dietary treatments did not significantly alter postmortem physicochemical meat quality parameters, including drip loss, cooking loss, Warner–Bratzler shear force, or muscle fatty acid profiles. Conclusion Combined dietary supplementation with biogenic ADS18 selenium and vitamin E effectively enhances tissue Se accumulation, optimizes systemic lipid status, and upregulates key selenoprotein gene expression in spent laying hens, without negatively affecting or altering fundamental postmortem meat quality characteristics. Implications These findings demonstrate that biogenic selenium produced by Stenotrophomonas maltophilia (ADS18), when co-supplemented with vitamin E, serves as an efficient nutritional strategy to enhance tissue selenium bioaccumulation, optimize lipid profiles, and upregulate key selenoprotein gene expression in aging spent laying hens. This provides the poultry industry with a sustainable bio-additive alternative to improve metabolic health and functional product value without compromising commercial meat quality attributes.

papers.title: Decoding Ferroptosis: Mechanistic Insights and Future Directions in the Precision Analysis of Lipid Hydroperoxides
papers.authors: Junya Ito
papers.abstract: Abstract Ferroptosis is a regulated form of cell death driven by iron-dependent lipid peroxidation of polyunsaturated phospholipids. While its core regulatory axis involving glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) and glutathione has been extensively studied, emerging evidence highlights the presence of multiple parallel defense systems. In addition, recent findings identify peroxiredoxin 6 as a critical regulator of intracellular selenium utilization, linking selenium metabolism to GPX4 biosynthesis and ferroptosis sensitivity. Despite these advances, a comprehensive understanding of ferroptosis mechanisms requires precise characterization of lipid hydroperoxides, the primary executioners of this cell death pathway. Here, we review the molecular basis of ferroptosis and its multilayered defense networks, with a particular focus on analytical challenges in lipid peroxidation research. We highlight recent progress in mass spectrometry–based approaches, including alkali metal adduction strategies, which enable positional isomer–resolved analysis of lipid hydroperoxides.

papers.title: Heat-dependent engagement of a buried mitophagy motif in prohibitin 2
papers.authors: Nan, J.; Yang, X.; Lin, Y.; Shao, Z.; Wang, X.; Wang, B.; Zhao, D.; Liu, B.
papers.abstract: Mitophagy receptors are generally switched on by upstream enzymes rather than by the receptor itself. Whether a receptor can instead respond directly to a physical stimulus has not been established. Here we show that a second LC3-interacting region (LIR) in prohibitin 2 (PHB2) is regulated by temperature. It lies in a marginally stable helix that holds its two anchor residues about 5 angstrom apart, whereas a bound LIR spans about 9 angstrom. Replica-scaling simulations showed that this helix, but not a matched control from the same protein under identical scaling, samples that geometry; purified PHB2 bound ATG8-family proteins only at 313 K and above. Substitutions designed from this geometry to stabilise (K253A/R255A) or destabilise (I254G) the helix altered binding, mitochondrial recruitment and respiration in PHB2-null cardiomyocytes. Mice carrying the stabilising substitutions in cardiomyocytes sustained greater cardiac injury during heat stroke despite matched thermal load and comparable systemic injury. Motif accessibility may therefore be a regulated variable rather than a fixed property of a fold.
