papers.title: First-principles analysis of the metal-free H2 dissociation mechanism by semiquinone radicals in mitochondrial Complex I and III.
papers.authors: Toru Ishibashi; Enjuro Harunari
papers.abstract: Although ameliorative effects of molecular hydrogen (H2) have been reported in a wide range of pathological conditions, an unresolved issue is the molecular mechanism by which H2 is activated in animal cells, which lack the metal hydrogenases that dissociate the exceptionally strong nonpolar H-H bond. Using first-principles calculations (geometries optimized with spin-unrestricted B3LYP-D3BJ/def2-SVP/CPCM and energies evaluated with ωB97M-V/def2-TZVPP) with the active-site clusters of the Q-chamber of mitochondrial respiratory-chain Complex I (PDB 7QSK) and the Qo site of Complex III (PDB 1PP9), this study examined whether semiquinone could directly dissociate H2 in the low-dielectric environment buried within the enzyme and examined what changes when a conserved residue is added as a second hydrogen atom acceptor. At both sites, the anionic semiquinone Q˙- had no reaction pathway for cleaving H-H, and only the neutral QH˙, protonated by nearby residues, opened a homolytic hydrogen atom transfer (HAT) pathway with a well-defined transition state and a bound product. The continuous shift in the spin density on the transferring hydrogen from nearly 0 in the reactant to +0.99 for free H˙ confirmed, at the electronic level, that this is a true homolytic HAT and neither a proton transfer nor a hydride transfer. The reaction energies (+21 to +26 kcal mol-1) agree with an estimate based on the difference between the bond dissociation free energies (BDFEs) of the O-H bond of ubiquinol QH2 and the H-H bond that is broken. The same BDFE comparison also makes QH˙ a spin-allowed hydrogen-atom abstractor superior to superoxide by about 30 kcal mol-1. For HAT with a single hydrogen atom acceptor, the reaction energy of QH˙ + H2 → QH2 + H˙ is +28.3 kcal mol-1, and the barrier cannot fall below this value. In the Q-chamber, the conserved Tyr108 residue can act as a second acceptor, and for hydrogen atom transfer with H2 held between QH˙ and TyrO˙, the barrier falls to +27.0 kcal mol-1. However, this reactive QH˙ arises only under hyper-reductive pressure, where quinone-pool overreduction and high membrane potential coincide, upon occupation and protonation at the buried semiquinone reaction site. Therefore, H2 dissociation itself is established only when the semiquinone reaction-site environment under hyper-reductive pressure is present as a necessary condition. Because H2 possesses one of the strongest σ bonds, the barrier is high and sharp, and quantum tunnelling makes a substantial contribution to crossing it at body temperature. At the one-dimensional Eckart level, this contribution does not exceed thermal activation, and it is obtained as a lower bound. The crossover temperatures, set by the imaginary frequency at the saddle, are 293.9 K for Complex I and 264.7 K for Complex III. The buried semiquinone reaction site makes a barrier against one of the strongest known σ bonds, which is thin enough to bring the crossover temperature to within 16 K of body temperature, and is itself a quantitative result of the study. The Marcus inverted region (bell-shaped kinetics) that we observed in solution in the previous work shows that H2 can be activated under metal-free conditions, but in that case, it is the electron that tunnels, moving along a coordinate distinct from the hydrogen nucleus analysed here. For the in-enzyme mechanism, the moderate primary isotope effect predicted at the same level (kH/kD ≈ 4) could be tested by detecting dissociated deuterium using D2 as a tracer. Taken together, the above results shift the mechanistic account of H2 medicine from classical antioxidant scavenging to redox regulation as a quantum-tunnelling-assisted conditional hydrogenase activity conditioned by reductive pressure and position it as a field of quantum biology.

papers.title: Food Contaminant Deoxynivalenol Causes Muscle Damage by Inducing Lipid Peroxidation and Ferroptosis
papers.authors: Bingxuan Jia; Huikang Lin; Yingzhu Tan; Aibo Wu
papers.venue: Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry
papers.abstract: Abstract Deoxynivalenol (DON) is a prevalent food contaminant that has been proposed to exert myotoxicity, but direct experimental validation remains insufficient. In this study, we used pig models and cell lines to investigate DON-induced muscle toxicity. In vivo, DON exposure leads to pathological muscle injury, disrupts energy metabolism, alters fatty acid metabolism, promotes the generation of lipid peroxides, and elevates Fe2+ levels. Cellular assays further confirmed that exposure to DON increases intracellular Fe2+ levels, inhibits the glutathione antioxidant pathway, and promotes lipid remodeling, ultimately facilitating lipid peroxidation and triggering ferroptosis. Cellular supplementation with complex lipids and free fatty acids improved C2C12 cell viability, which may be achieved by maintaining membrane lipid homeostasis. Collectively, this study demonstrates that DON induces muscle damage associated with lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis, which may offer a promising direction for the development of protective intervention strategies.

papers.title: Gastrodin combined with donepezil alleviates cognitive dysfunction in Alzheimer’s disease mice by improving mitochondrial function through AMPK/PGC-1α/SIRT3 axis
papers.authors: Junwen Wang; Jing Wu; Fenrong Liang; Shulei Huang; Longfei Liu; Ying Huang; Yiming Wang
papers.abstract: Objective This study aims to explore whether gastrodin (Gas) combined with donepezil (Don) has a neuroprotective effect on Alzheimer’s disease (AD) mice by regulating the AMPK/PGC-1α/SIRT3 signaling axis. Methods HT22 cells were transfected with SIRT3 siRNA or control siRNA. Cells were then treated with the AMPK inhibitor, Don, Gas, or their combination. Subsequently, HT22 cells were treated with Amyloid beta 1–42 (Aβ 1–42) to induce an in vitro AD model. Cell viability was detected by CCK8 assay. DCFH-DA fluorescent probe was used to evaluate cell reactive oxygen species (ROS). Adenosine triphosphate (ATP) content was detected by luciferase chemiluminescence method. Cell membrane potential was measured by flow cytometry. For in vivo experiments, WT mice and APP/PS1 mice were treated with Don, Gas or a combination of drugs. Morris water maze test, Y-maze test and novel object recognition test were used to evaluate the cognitive impairment of mice. The pathological changes of hippocampus were detected by HE staining, and the expression of Aβ protein in hippocampus and cortex was detected by IHC. In addition, the protein and mRNA expressions of APP, Tau, and AMPK/PGC-1α/SIRT3 signaling axis were determined by Western blot and RT-QPCR. Results Gas combined with Don significantly improved cognitive dysfunction, reduced Aβ plaque deposition in the cortex and hippocampus, up-regulated AMPK/PGC-1α/SIRT3 axis, and inhibited the abnormal phosphorylation of Tau and APP in APP/PS1 mice compared with the model group and the Don group ( p < 0.05). In vitro cell experiments confirmed that the combination of the two drugs could improve cell viability, inhibit cell apoptosis, restore ATP level, reduce ROS accumulation, stabilize mitochondrial membrane potential, and improve mitochondrial function ( p < 0.05). Molecular experiments and complementary experiments showed that Gas combined with Don activated AMPK/PGC-1α/SIRT3 signaling axis ( p < 0.05). Silencing SIRT3 or inhibiting AMPK could reverse the protective effect of the combined regimen ( p < 0.05). Conclusion Gas combined with Don can maintain mitochondrial homeostasis through AMPK/PGC-1α/SIRT3 pathway, alleviate AD-relaated pathological damage, and exert neuroprotection.

papers.title: Insights into CD36/P-gp involvement in dietary lipid-driven PAH transport across the blood-brain barrier.
papers.authors: Xiaofang Liu; Jie Zhu; Li Liang; Jixian Zhang; Chaoting Wen; Youdong Li; Guoyan Liu; Xin Xu
papers.abstract: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), as widespread environmental contaminants, exhibit neurotoxicity. Because PAHs often co-occur with dietary lipids in foods, those lipids might serve as vehicles that alter PAH biotransport and accumulation in the brain. In this work, we systematically investigated how three common dietary fatty acids-oleic acid, linoleic acid (LA), and linolenic acid-differently influence the transport steps (including cellular uptake, efflux, and clearance) of benzo[a]pyrene (BaP) and benzo[b]fluoranthene (BbF) across the blood-brain barrier, using a bEnd.3 cell-based model, and explored the potential underlying molecular mechanisms. Results revealed that dietary lipids, acting as carriers, significantly enhanced cellular uptake of PAHs, with LA increasing the uptake of BaP and BbF by 20.36% and 17.90%, respectively, and accelerated transmembrane transport dynamics. Simultaneously, distinct lipids differentially affected PAH clearance and efflux. Notably, LA delayed the clearance of PAHs, prolonging the elimination half-life of BaP from 10.117 h to 17.696 h and that of BbF from 7.418 h to 14.964 h, thereby increasing overall brain exposure. Mechanistically, LA was observed to upregulate the fatty acid transporter CD36, and functional inhibition studies suggested that P-glycoprotein and CD36 may jointly contribute to lipid-modulated effects. This study suggests that dietary lipids influence brain exposure to PAHs through a multi-level network, highlighting a factor that warrants consideration when assessing their neurotoxicity risks.

papers.title: ITGB1 Contributes to Matrix Stiffness–Induced Lipid Raft Organization and Promotes Hepatocellular Carcinoma Cell Migration
papers.authors: Xu Zhang; Xinyu Liu; Yan Liu; Guanbin Song
papers.abstract: Matrix stiffening is a characteristic pathological feature of the hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) microenvironment and promotes HCC cell migration. Lipid rafts are cholesterol–enriched plasma membrane microdomains involved in cell adhesion and migration. However, whether matrix stiffness promotes lipid raft organization and whether lipid rafts contribute to stiffness–promoted HCC cell migration remain unclear. Using two HCC cell lines cultured on polyacrylamide hydrogels with distinct stiffnesses, we found that stiff matrix enhanced cell migration, increased Area-normalized GM1 fluorescence, and upregulated Caveolin-1 and Flotillin-1 protein expression, consistent with enhanced lipid raft–associated membrane organization. Cholesterol depletion with methyl-β–cyclodextrin (MβCD) reduced GM1 fluorescence and attenuated migration on the Stiff matrix. Cholesterol replenishment partially restored GM1 fluorescence and wound closure after MβCD treatment. To explore how extracellular matrix stiffness is coupled to lipid raft organization, we next examined integrin β1 (ITGB1), a major extracellular matrix mechanoreceptor. The Stiff matrix increased ITGB1 protein expression, ITGB1–GM1 colocalization, and ITGB1 levels in raft-enriched fractions. ITGB1 knockdown reduced GM1 fluorescence, decreased Caveolin-1 and Flotillin-1 levels in raft-enriched fractions, and suppressed migration under Stiff–matrix conditions. These findings support a contributory role for ITGB1 in stiffness-associated lipid raft organization and HCC cell migration.

papers.title: Magnoflorine Ameliorates MASH in Mice Fed a High‐Fat and High‐Fructose Diet by Promoting AMPK ‐Mediated Lipophagy and Fatty Acid Oxidation
papers.authors: Zhengjie Lu; Tongyun Mao; Longxin Chai; Kaiqi Chen; Kexin Liu; Cong Zhang; Hao Kou
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Emerging as a significant clinical burden, metabolic dysfunction‐associated steatohepatitis (MASH) continues to challenge global healthcare systems due to limited effective interventions. Magnoflorine, a naturally occurring quaternary aporphine alkaloid abundant in dietary botanicals, has demonstrated promising hypolipidemic and anti‐inflammatory properties in preliminary investigations. This investigation systematically evaluated both the therapeutic potential and mechanistic pathways underlying the capacity of magnoflorine to ameliorate MASH‐associated hepatic pathologies. Male C57BL/6 mice received 12‐week high‐fat and high‐fructose diet (HFFD) induction to establish MASH models, with graded magnoflorine dosing. Through integrated histopathology (H&E/ORO/Masson), transcriptomics, and targeted interventions at both cellular and animal levels, we elucidated the therapeutic mechanisms of magnoflorine. Results showed that magnoflorine effectively alleviated hepatic steatosis, inflammation, and fibrosis in HFFD‐fed mice. Mechanistically, RNA‐seq revealed that the 5′‐monophosphate AMP‐activated protein kinase (AMPK) activation was the central pathway mediating the effects of magnoflorine to impede MASH progression. Furthermore, AMPKα activation induced by magnoflorine stimulated hepatic lipophagy in HFFD‐fed mice, which further affected lipid β‐oxidation and inflammation. The findings were consistent in HepG2 cells incubated with palmitic acid. In vitro, silencing AMPKα reversed the stimulatory effect of magnoflorine on lipophagy in HepG2 cells. In vivo, liver‐specific AMPKα silencing in mice blocked the enhancement of hepatic lipophagy and the improvement of MASH caused by magnoflorine. In brief, this study indicates that magnoflorine improves MASH in mice by activating hepatic lipophagy via AMPKα‐dependent effects. This discovery provides a novel potential therapeutic alternative for MASH.

papers.title: Maternal Genetic Diversity and Population Structure of Four Jordanian Subpopulations Revealed by Mitochondrial DNA Variation
papers.authors: Almuthanna K. Alkaraki; Hiba T. Alqaissi; Tuqa R. Abu-Alhayjaa; Eman N. Alabbas; Reham I. Ghawanmeh; Mohammad B. Alsliman; Mazhar S. Al Zoubi
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Jordan’s geographical position at the crossroads of the Southern Levant, Arabian Peninsula, and Africa has contributed to its complex demographic and population interactions and genetic admixture. This study aimed to investigate the maternal genetic structure among four Jordanian subpopulations: Fellahin (Farmers), Bedouins (Nomads), Alnawar (Banu Murra), and Beer Al-Saba Bedouins. Methods: A total of 192 unrelated participants, 48 from each subpopulation, were analyzed after required ethical approvals. Three mitochondrial DNA regions (the D-loop, cytochrome b, and cytochrome c oxidase subunit 1) were amplified and sequenced. The predicted maternal haplogroups were assigned using the online HaploGrep 3 tool. Further genetic structure and diversity analyses were assessed through Multidimensional Scaling (MDS) analysis based on the FST distance matrix, along with a Principal Coordinate Analysis (PCoA). The studied subpopulations were also compared with other populations from the Levant, the Arabian Peninsula, North Africa, East and West Africa, and Europe. Results: The most frequent predicted haplogroup was U in Fellahin (18.75%) and Bedouins (22.92%), H in Alnawar (Banu Murra) (18.75%), and U in Beer Al-Saba Bedouins (20.83%). Maternal genetic diversity was high among the four studied subpopulations, with an average value of 0.9. MDS analysis placed the Jordanian subpopulations within the broader maternal genetic landscape of the Levant and Arabian Peninsula, while also revealing population-specific differentiation, particularly among the Bedouins of Beer Al-Saba. PCoA further showed substantial overlap among Fellahin and Bedouins, partial differentiation of Beer Al-Saba Bedouins, and broader dispersion among Alnawar (Banu Murra) individuals. Interestingly, in comparison with selected Roma subgroups, Alnawar (Banu Murra) showed greater similarity in the predicted mitochondrial haplogroup composition with other Jordanian groups than most of the selected Roma reference populations. Conclusions: The obtained results showed substantial maternal genetic diversity within the studied Jordanian subgroups and highlight the influence of distinct demographic histories on the mitochondrial variation. The study also provides additional mtDNA data that may support future development of population-specific mitochondrial reference datasets for forensic applications in Jordan.

papers.title: Mechanistic study on the promotion of osteogenic differentiation in osteoporotic rats by moxibustion via regulation of BMSCs-derived exosomal miR-27a-3p-mediated mitophagy.
papers.authors: Xing Li; Xiao Li; Adi Wirawan Tjahjono; Xiaoli Chen; Lu Cui; Paradi Sangvatanakul; Xiaojuan Hong; Xiang Li
papers.abstract: AIMS: To investigate the effects of moxibustion (MOX) on bone loss and osteogenic differentiation in ovariectomized (OVX) rats and determine whether these effects are mediated by mitophagy through bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs)-derived exosomal miR-27a-3p. METHODS: The study was conducted in three stages. In stage 1, sham-operated (SO), OVX, and OVX + MOX rats were evaluated by micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) to assess bone mass and by Alizarin Red S (ARS) staining to evaluate osteogenic differentiation. Autophagy-related markers were also examined, and mitochondrial-lysosomal colocalization was assessed by immunofluorescence. In stage 2, the mitophagy inhibitor Mdivi-1 was administered to OVX + MOX rats to determine the contribution of mitophagy to the effects of MOX. Sequencing analysis and TargetScan prediction identified a potential regulatory relationship between miR-27a-3p and the mitophagy-related gene PINK1, which was subsequently validated using a dual-luciferase reporter assay. In stage 3, miR-27a-3p agomir and antagomir were used to investigate the involvement of the miR-27a-3p-mitophagy axis. RESULTS: MOX increased bone mineral density, improved bone microarchitecture, and enhanced osteogenic differentiation in OVX rats, accompanied by increased mitophagy. Mdivi-1 attenuated these beneficial effects, exacerbating bone loss and reducing osteogenic gene expression, mineralized nodule formation, mitochondrial membrane potential, and mitophagy. The dual-luciferase reporter assay confirmed that PINK1 is a direct target of miR-27a-3p. Inhibition of miR-27a-3p with an antagomir impaired bone microarchitecture, mitophagy, and osteogenesis. Conversely, MOX produced effects comparable to those of the miR-27a-3p agomir, with both interventions promoting osteogenic differentiation through the miR-27a-3p-mitophagy axis. CONCLUSIONS: MOX attenuates bone loss in OVX-induced osteoporosis (OP) by promoting osteogenic differentiation. These effects may be mediated, at least in part, by activation of mitophagy through the BMSCs-associated miR-27a-3p/PINK1 axis, providing a potential mechanistic basis for the therapeutic effects of MOX in OP.

papers.title: Microwave-assisted stabilization of lipid-rich melon seed powder: enzyme inactivation, oxidative stability, and quality changes during storage
papers.authors: Gulcin Yildiz; Gökçen Yıldız
papers.venue: Frontiers in Food Science and Technology
papers.abstract: This study investigated the effectiveness of microwave-assisted stabilization in reducing endogenous enzyme activities, delaying lipid deterioration, and preserving the quality of lipid-rich melon seed powder (MSP). A 3 × 3 factorial design comprising three microwave power levels (100, 200, and 300 W) and three treatment durations (30, 60, and 90 s) was employed. Nine microwave treatments and an untreated control were evaluated for lipase and lipoxygenase (LOX) activities, physicochemical characteristics, antioxidant activity, and functional properties. Storage stability was assessed over 60 days by monitoring free fatty acid (FFA) content, peroxide value (PV), and thiobarbituric acid reactive substances (TBARS). Among the tested conditions, MW8 (300 W × 60 s; nominal specific energy input of 360 J/g) achieved the greatest enzyme inactivation, reducing lipase and LOX activities by 78.2% and 69.0%, respectively. After 60 days of storage, MW8 exhibited substantially lower FFA content (2.45% versus 5.65%), PV (5.97 versus 12.80 meq O 2 /kg sample), and TBARS (1.02 versus 2.18 µM MDA/g sample) than the untreated control. MW8 also increased total phenolic content and DPPH radical-scavenging activity while improving water and oil absorption capacities. Extending the treatment duration to 90 s at 300 W did not provide additional enzyme inactivation or storage protection, demonstrating a non-linear response to microwave treatment severity. Overall, microwave treatment at 300 W for 60 s provided the most favorable balance between enzyme inactivation, delayed lipid deterioration, and preservation of the evaluated quality characteristics under the investigated experimental conditions.

papers.title: Mitochondrial stress-signaling networks in male reproductive dysfunction: redox, inflammatory, and cell-death integration with context-dependent modulation by melatonin
papers.authors: Qi Qi; Jingsheng Luo; Xuejiao Ren; Lin Jiang; Tianhui Liu; Wei Liu; ChangJie Bao; Meiyan Sun; Hongxun Fu
papers.abstract: Mitochondria integrate bioenergetic, redox, calcium, inflammatory, and cell-death signals during cellular stress, but their position within male reproductive injury is highly dependent on cell type and initiating insult. This critical narrative review examines mitochondrial stress-signaling networks in Leydig cells, Sertoli cells, developing germ cells, and spermatozoa, with particular attention to their context-dependent modulation by melatonin. Physiological reactive oxygen species (ROS) participate in steroidogenesis and sperm function, whereas excessive or mislocalized ROS can interact bidirectionally with mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammatory signaling, impaired quality control, and regulated cell death. Across toxicant, metabolic, inflammatory, thermal, ischemic, aging, and cryopreservation models, mitochondria can therefore function as conditional integrative signaling hubs rather than universal initiating causes. Melatonin-associated responses intersect with these networks through MT1/MT2 signaling, redox-sensitive processes, chemical interactions with reactive species, and mitochondria-associated mechanisms, with reported effects on mitochondrial function, inflammatory amplification, apoptosis, and ferroptosis- or pyroptosis-associated injury. However, molecular co-variation is distinguished from causal signaling, and lipid peroxidation or inflammasome activation alone is not considered definitive evidence of ferroptosis or pyroptosis. Human evidence remains limited relative to animal, ex vivo, and cell-culture studies. We propose an evidence-calibrated initiation–amplification–progression framework in which mitochondria integrate stress signals dynamically and melatonin acts as a context-dependent experimental modulator rather than an established reproductive therapy.

papers.title: Mitochondrialny wymiennik Na⁺/Ca²⁺ NCLX w regulacji homeostazy wapniowej i patofizjologii chorób: mechanizmy, kontrowersje i perspektywy badań The mitochondrial Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger NCLX in calcium homeostasis and disease pathophysiology: mechanisms, controversies and research perspectives
papers.authors: Katarzyna Romaniuk
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial calcium homeostasis is an important regulator of bioenergetics, redox balance and cell survival. This review discusses the structure, regulation and pathophysiological significance of the mitochondrial Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger NCLX, encoded by the SLC8B1 gene. Particular attention is paid to the role of NCLX in Ca²⁺ efflux from the mitochondrial matrix, integration of Na⁺–Ca²⁺–ROS signaling, and cellular responses to metabolic stress, hypoxia and mitochondrial injury. The available data indicate that NCLX dysfunction contributes to the pathophysiology of neurodegenerative, cardiovascular, metabolic, inflammatory and neoplastic diseases. However, the function of this transporter strongly depends on cell type, duration of stress and the degree of mitochondrial Ca²⁺ overload. Therefore, NCLX should be considered a regulator of mitochondrial function whose diagnostic, prognostic and therapeutic relevance requires further validation in experimental and clinical studies.

papers.title: Multi-scale effects of single-dose psilocybin in the macaque brain
papers.authors: Jiaojian Wang; Jin Chen; Wenjie Sun; Zeyuan Yang; Chengsi Luo; Futing Yang; Yu-Xuan Zhu; Hongshuang Wang; Xihan Zhang; Jamie Masthay; Soo-Ji Baek; Jie Li; Yan Zhuo; Xiaopeng Wang; Yashi Wu; Yingzi Ma; Qinyao Sun; Weizhi Ji; Steve Chang; Xiaohui Wang; Xiaona Zhu; Ji Hu; Yongchang Chen; Tifei Yuan
papers.abstract: Abstract Psilocybin holds strong therapeutic promise for treating major depressive disorder. However, the cellular and molecular substrates underlying its action have not been fully elucidated, especially in the primate brain. We combined multimodal MRI, magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS), cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) proteomics and metabolomics, and single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) to map the multiscale temporospatial dynamics induced by a single dose of psilocybin in cynomolgus macaques. Psilocybin increased the integration of the frontoparietal network (FPN) with the default-mode and limbic networks, transiently reduced integration of the FPN with the somatomotor network, and induced global network segregation. Several regions in the cortex, striatum, and thalamus as well as certain of the frontoparietal white matter pathways showed persistent enhancement lasting 1 week. Notably, these changes were accompanied by a CSF multi-omics shift from acute prostaglandin-dominated inflammation to a sustained enrichment of an omega-3 fatty acid-associated anti-inflammatory state together with a bidirectional reorganization of extracellular matrix (ECM)-related signatures, characterized by increased CD44 and decreased fibulin-family proteins. In addition, we found lasting upregulation of TCA-cycle and NAD(P)-dependent redox enzymes. This was further supported by sustained elevations of glutamate/glutamine and total creatine in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC), which was found using in vivo MRS. At the cellular level, psilocybin promoted HTR2A selective upregulation in deep-layer excitatory neurons along with a widespread enhancement of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation centered on the complex I subunit ND3 across diverse excitatory and inhibitory neuronal subtypes in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. Glial-state remodeling, including a shift of astrocytes toward ECM remodeling states and microglia toward an anti-inflammatory state, also occurred. Collectively, these findings provide evidence in the primate brain that psilocybin induces functional integration and segregation of brain networks, enhances energy metabolism and synaptic plasticity, and modulates neuroimmune signaling. All the data will be shared as an integrated resource for primate psilocybin research.

papers.title: Natural Medicines Targeting Mitochondrial Dysfunction in Spinocerebellar Ataxia Type 3: A Narrative Review of Cellular and Molecular Events
papers.authors: Mwafaq Kmail; Noor Asyikin Suaidi; Jin Han Chin; Lee Wei Lim; Kah Hui Wong
papers.abstract: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 (SCA3), also known as Machado-Joseph disease, is the most common autosomal dominant spinocerebellar ataxia and is characterized by progressive neurodegeneration for which no Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved therapeutics are currently available. Mitochondrial dysfunction has emerged as a central pathogenic mechanism in SCA3, making it a promising therapeutic target. This narrative review aims to evaluate the published evidence on the therapeutic potential of natural medicines and their active compounds targeting mitochondrial dysfunction in SCA3. This review summarizes published evidence on the therapeutic potential of natural medicines and their active compounds targeting mitochondrial dysfunction in SCA3 in preclinical studies. The reviewed studies suggest the therapeutic potential of Glycyrrhiza inflata, Codonopsis pilosula, Ginkgo biloba, Poria cocos, Pueraria lobata, Rehmannia glutinosa, Curcuma longa, Hericium erinaceus, Astragalus membranaceus, Hemerocallis citrina, caffeic acid, and resveratrol in targeting mitochondrial dysfunction in SCA3. These natural medicines were reported to regulate multiple mitochondrial-associated pathways, including oxidative stress, mitochondrial membrane potential, mitochondrial bioenergetics, mitochondrial dynamics, mitochondrial quality control, and mitochondria-mediated apoptosis, thereby improving neuronal survival and mitochondrial function in experimental SCA3 models. In conclusion, natural medicines targeting mitochondrial dysfunction represent promising preclinical candidates for further investigation in SCA3. However, further mechanistic investigations, well-designed clinical trials, and optimization of pharmacokinetic properties are required to facilitate their translation into clinical practice.

papers.title: Piezoelectric Tm‐ZnO Nanoparticles Reprogram Neutrophils by Modulating Mitochondrial Homeostasis for Osteoarthritis Therapy
papers.authors: Chengxiao Liu; Ruqi Wang; Zhaowenbin Zhang; Ruiqing Wang; Xiaowei Wu; Yuxuan Liu; Zhengliang Wang; Ruomei Li; Chunlong Zhang; Bin Li; Bing Fang; Chen Yang; Lunguo Xia
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Osteoarthritis (OA) is increasingly recognized as a chronic inflammatory disorder driven by immune dysregulation, with early neutrophil infiltration associated with a pro‐inflammatory phenotype and disrupted mitochondrial homeostasis. However, whether restoring neutrophil mitochondrial function can reprogram their inflammatory state and ameliorate OA remains unclear. Distinct from previous piezoelectric strategies for OA that primarily focus on chondrocytes or macrophages, this study focuses on neutrophil mitochondrial immunometabolism. Here, we report piezoelectric thulium‐doped zinc oxide (Tm‐ZnO) nanoparticles that associate with neutrophil mitochondria to restore mitochondrial homeostasis and reprogram neutrophil polarization. The ultrasmall size and positive surface charge of Tm‐ZnO facilitate mitochondrial association, while its enhanced piezoelectric properties (14‐fold increase in piezoelectric coefficient) enable activation by low‐intensity pulsed ultrasound (LIPUS), generating localized bioelectric cues. This stimulation reduces mitochondrial ROS, enhances oxidative phosphorylation, and is associated with suppression of HIF‐1/NF‐κB signaling, thereby promoting neutrophil polarization from a pro‐inflammatory N1 state toward a reparative N2 phenotype. In vitro and in vivo, Tm‐ZnO+LIPUS attenuates synovial inflammation, restores chondrocyte anabolic activity, limits matrix degradation, and facilitates cartilage repair. Together, these findings establish a mitochondria‐associated piezoelectric strategy for bioelectric reprogramming of neutrophil immunometabolism and highlight its therapeutic potential for OA and other chronic inflammatory diseases.

papers.title: PPARγ/P21 Signaling Mediates Butyrate-Driven Protection against Aging-Related Endothelial Dysfunction: A Novel Effect of Soybean Polysaccharide via the Gut-Vascular Axis.
papers.authors: Qile Zhang; Zhengming Zhou; Hoi Wa Yeung; Yiu Ming Cheung; Yuen Lam Wong; Chufeng He; Shouhe Huang; Lu Jiang; Xiao Yu Tian; Zhen-Yu Chen; Wing Tak Wong
papers.venue: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
papers.abstract: Aging-induced endothelial dysfunction is a core driver of age-related cardiovascular diseases (CVDs). In 20-month-old naturally aged mice, 12-week soybean polysaccharide (SP) supplementation restored endothelium-dependent relaxation, reduced aortic reactive oxygen species and VCAM-1 in the aortic endothelium, and attenuated colon senescence, improved gut barrier integrity, and reduced systemic inflammation, as shown by decreased serum LPS, IL-1β, TNF-α, and fecal and serum TMA/TMAO levels. SP enriched butyrate-producing gut bacteria, including Lachnospiraceae_NK4A136_group, and increased gut and serum butyrate, consistent with enhanced microbial short-chain fatty acid biosynthesis capacity predicted by PICRUSt2. Direct butyrate supplementation reproduced these vascular and colonic benefits. It activated PPARγ signaling and downregulated p21, ICAM-1, VCAM-1, and p16, whereas PPARα and PPARδ remained unchanged. These findings support a gut microbiota-butyrate-PPARγ/p21 axis through which SP protects against aging-related endothelial dysfunction, providing a nutritional basis for targeting the gut-vascular axis in cardiovascular aging.

papers.title: Role and mechanism of action of PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy in nonylphenol-induced podocyte apoptosis and glomerulonephritis.
papers.authors: Chengxing Wang; Jie Xu; Yuzhu Xu; Ya Luo; Jie Yu
papers.abstract: Podocyte injury is an early and critical event in the development of glomerulonephritis (GN). Nonylphenol (NP) can accumulate in the kidney and induce nephrotoxicity. However, the mechanism by which NP promotes GN progression by inducing podocyte apoptosis remains unclear. This study aimed to determine whether NP exposure activated PTEN-induced kinase 1/Parkin RBR E3 ubiquitin protein ligase (PINK1/Parkin)-mediated mitophagy, leading to mitochondrial homeostasis imbalance in podocytes and promoting apoptosis, thereby inducing pathological changes associated with GN in mice. Cell experiments were performed in Mouse Podocyte Clone-5 (MPC-5) cells by activating or inhibiting Parkin. In vivo, 72 male wild-type and Parkin-/- C57BL/6 mice were treated with different doses of NP by gavage for 90 days to investigate the role of Parkin in NP-induced renal injury. The results showed that NP exposure activated the PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy pathway in MPC-5 cells and was accompanied by increased apoptosis and inflammatory responses. Parkin inhibition impaired mitophagy and exacerbated NP-induced cellular injury, whereas Parkin activation enhanced mitophagy and attenuated inflammation and apoptosis, indicating a cytoprotective role of Parkin. Consistently, NP exposure for 90 days induced renal dysfunction, podocyte injury, mitochondrial ultrastructural damage, inflammation, apoptosis, and activation of the PINK1/Parkin pathway in mice. These alterations were further aggravated in Parkin-/- mice, which exhibited impaired autophagy and more severe mitochondrial and renal injury. Collectively, Parkin-mediated mitophagy plays a key protective role in maintaining podocyte homeostasis and alleviating glomerular structural and functional damage.

papers.title: Securing Maternal Identity: Halachic Concerns in the Age of Mitochondrial Replacement Therapy
papers.authors: John Loike; Tzvi Flaum; Alan Kadish
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial replacement therapy (MRT) encompasses assisted reproductive technologies designed to prevent the transmission of pathogenic mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) mutations by combining the DNA in the nucleus (nuclear genome) of the intending parents with another woman’s enucleated egg that provides healthy donor-derived mtDNA. The use of advanced genomic engineering in MRT raises distinct ethical and halachic considerations regarding the ontological status of embryos containing genetic material from more than two individuals. This paper advances an original theoretical protocol, termed biparental mitochondrial replacement therapy (Bi-MRT), that mitigates the central halachic concerns associated with multi-parent embryos. In this protocol, future advances in stem cell technology could be employed to generate an enucleated gamete-like cell containing healthy mitochondria from the husband. The meiotic spindle–chromosome complex from the wife’s oocyte could then be transplanted into this reconstituted gamete, which could be subsequently fertilized with the husband’s sperm for IVF. If technically feasible and developmentally competent, the resulting embryo could potentially be transferred to the wife for gestation. By combining the wife’s nuclear genetic contribution, gestation, and parturition with the husband’s paternal DNA, this framework isolates the third-party mitochondrial contribution as a non-maternal factor, thereby reinforcing the wife’s singular claim to halachic maternity. Biparental MRT therefore represents a theoretical framework that could potentially reduce some halachic concerns associated with conventional MRT, but substantial scientific and safety barriers remain before any clinical application could be contemplated.

papers.title: Small-Molecule Inhibitors of Cholesterol Sulfotransferase as Immunomodulatory Agents
papers.authors: Lindsay E. Boudreau; Amanda J. Smith; Hyang Yeon Lee; Bidisha Chakraborty; Kyle R. Abo; Kenneth Chen; Satish K. Nair; Paul J. Hergenrother
papers.abstract: Abstract Though immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) therapy has been a promising advance in cancer treatment, response rates to ICB are low owing to other mechanisms that cancers employ to evade the immune system. SULT2B1b is an enzyme known to produce cholesterol sulfate (CS), an immunosuppressive metabolite that inhibits T-cell migration. Cancers expressing high levels of SULT2B1b thus generate a tumor microenvironment that excludes T cells, which leads to increased tumor growth and renders ICB therapy ineffective. Here, we identify a novel class of azasteroid SULT2B1b inhibitors with greater potency and selectivity than previously identified compounds. X-ray co-crystal structures indicate that these inhibitors bind in a conformation different from that of native substrates, enabling inhibition without acting as a substrate. Additionally, these new compounds effectively reduce CS levels in tumors in mice and, as such, have potential as cancer therapeutics in combination with ICB therapy.

papers.title: Therapeutic effect of quercetin on airway remodeling of ovalbumin-induced asthmatic mice via inhibition of the mtDNA-cGAS-STING pathway.
papers.authors: Rihuang Qiu; Zhiwen Liu; Pingkang Li; Laishui Peng; Yuhui Xu; Yiming Zeng
papers.abstract: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory airway disease with limited treatments for airway remodeling. Quercetin has anti-inflammatory potential, but whether it acts through the mtDNA-cGAS-STING pathway remains unclear. This study aimed to explore the therapeutic effect of quercetin on asthma in a mouse model and the associated underlying molecular mechanism. Various doses of quercetin were employed to intervene in a mouse model of asthma. Alterations in inflammation-related indicators and mtDNA in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF), pathological changes in lung tissue, and activation of the cGAS-STING signaling pathway were detected. The STING agonist DMXAA was utilized to verify whether quercetin could enhance the relevant indicators in the mouse asthma model by suppressing the activation of the mtDNA-cGAS-STING signaling pathway. Finally, BEAS-2B cells were treated with TGF-β to mimic the epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) process of asthmatic epithelial cells. Quercetin, a STING overexpression vector and ethidium bromide intervention were used to analyze whether quercetin inhibited the TGF-β-induced EMT process in BEAS-2B cells by suppressing the mtDNA-cGAS-STING signaling pathway. Quercetin treatment effectively mitigated inflammatory infiltration and airway remodeling in a mouse model of asthma, and the therapeutic effect was most pronounced at a high dose. Additionally, quercetin treatment inhibited the activation of the mtDNA-cGAS-STING signaling pathway in asthmatic mice. Treatment with DMXAA reversed the therapeutic effect of quercetin in the mouse model of asthma. At the cellular level, quercetin inhibited TGF-β-induced EMT in BEAS-2B cells by suppressing the mtDNA-cGAS-STING signaling pathway. Thus, quercetin can ameliorate inflammatory infiltration and airway remodeling in a mouse model of asthma, potentially by suppressing the activation of the mtDNA-cGAS-STING signaling pathway.

papers.title: The nonsense-mediated decay RNA-surveillance pathway facilitates the hypoxia response by C. elegans.
papers.authors: Calista Diehl; H Robert Horvitz
papers.abstract: Hypoxia (decreased O2) induces physiological, metabolic, and behavioral changes. The major hypoxia response pathway is conserved from nematodes to mammals and is driven by activation of the HIF (hypoxia inducible factor) family of transcription factors. Despite a fundamental role of the HIF pathway in regulating cellular homeostasis in response to hypoxic stress, interactions between the HIF pathway and cellular quality control pathways are largely unknown. Using an unbiased genetic screen, we found that in C. elegans nonsense-mediated decay (NMD), an evolutionarily conserved mechanism of RNA surveillance, acts in parallel to HIF-1 to selectively enhance specific aspects of the response to HIF-1 activation, possibly through coregulation of a distinct subset of HIF-1-up-regulated genes. Our findings reveal a functional integration between oxygen sensing and RNA surveillance and establish NMD as a key regulator of specific aspects of the HIF-1-driven transcriptional program and physiological response.

papers.title: Alginate Oligosaccharide Alleviates Age-Related Hearing Loss via TFEB-Associated Autophagy Restoration to Attenuate Oxidative Stress and Inflammation.
papers.authors: Shibo Su; Xinzhe Zhang; Meili Li; Peiyuan Zhang; Bailiu Ya; Wenjing Wang; Linghao Wang; Shuxuan Li; Hui Li; Xiaoyu Li; Jing Chen; Haiyan Yin
papers.venue: European journal of pharmaceutical sciences : official journal of the European Federation for Pharmaceutical Sciences
papers.abstract: Age-related hearing loss (ARHL) is a highly prevalent sensory disorder characterized by progressive cochlear degeneration. To date, no effective pharmacological treatment is clinically available. In this study, we investigated the otoprotective efficacy and underlying mechanisms of alginate oligosaccharide (AOS) against D-galactose (D-gal)-induced senescence in vitro and age-associated cochlear dysfunction in C57BL/6J mice. Multi-omics analyses identified oxidative stress, inflammation, cellular senescence, and autophagy, as core targeted pathways associated with AOS treatment. In D-gal-treated HEI-OC1 cells and cochlear explants, AOS treatment markedly reduced senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal) activity and downregulated senescence markers P16 and P21. These anti-senescent effects were accompanied by ameliorated oxidative and pro-inflammatory stress, as reflected by decreased reactive oxygen species (ROS), preserved mitochondrial function, and suppressed nuclear factor-κB/NOD-like receptor pyrin domain-containing 3 (NF-κB/NLRP3) signaling. AOS also promoted transcription factor EB (TFEB) nuclear translocation and attenuated D-gal-induced autophagy-related dysregulation. Pharmacological inhibition of autophagy and TFEB nuclear entry effectively blunted these cytoprotective, antioxidant, and anti-inflammatory benefits of AOS, supporting the involvement of TFEB-associated autophagic signaling in AOS-mediated protection. In C57BL/6J mice, long-term AOS administration significantly lowered auditory brainstem response (ABR) thresholds, attenuated the age-related degeneration of hair cells and spiral ganglion neurons, and reduced cochlear senescence markers. Furthermore, AOS suppressed MDA accumulation, elevated SOD activity, inhibited NF-κB/NLRP3 activation, and restored TFEB-associated autophagic homeostasis in vivo. Collectively, these findings suggest that AOS protects against age-associated cochlear dysfunction and senescence, accompanied by reduced oxidative stress and inflammation and improved autophagy-related homeostasis. TFEB-associated signaling may contribute to these protective effects, supporting further investigation of AOS for the prevention or delay of cochlear aging.

papers.title: Associations between air pollution, accelerated biological aging, and oral inflammatory diseases: evidence from the UK Biobank cohort
papers.authors: Hui Zhan; Dong Liu; You Guo; Wei Liu
papers.abstract: Background The relationships between air pollution exposure and incident risk of oral inflammatory diseases (OIDs) and roles of accelerated biological aging remain unclear. Methods In 348,247 adults from the UK Biobank, the individual levels of air pollutants, including particulate matter (PM) (PM 2.5 , PM 10 , PM 2.5–10, and PM 2.5 absorbance ), nitrogen dioxide (NO 2 ), nitric oxides (NO x ), and air pollution score (multiple air pollutants exposure), were estimated. The associations between air pollution exposure and incident risk of OIDs were assessed. The mediation roles of the Klemera–Doubal method biological age (KDM-BA) acceleration and the phenotypic age (PhenoAge) acceleration were evaluated. Results During the median follow-up of 16.49 years, a total of 3,967 incident OIDs were documented. Each one standard deviation increment in PM 2.5 , PM 10 , PM 2.5–10, PM 2.5 absorbance , NO 2 , NO x , and air pollution score was significantly associated with 8%, 4%, 3%, 5%, 10%, 8%, and 8% increments in incident risk of OIDs, respectively (all p < 0.05). All air pollutants except PM 2.5–10 were significantly and positively associated with KDM-BA acceleration, and all air pollutants were significantly and positively associated with PhenoAge acceleration (all p < 0.05). KDM-BA acceleration mediated the associations between all air pollution (except PM 2.5–10 ) and incident risk of OIDs, with mediation proportion ranging from 1.21 to 5.42%. PhenoAge acceleration mediated the associations between all air pollutants and incident risk of OIDs, with mediation proportion ranging from 8.52 to 16.65%. Conclusion Air pollution may contribute to increased incident risk of OIDs, and premature aging may play an important role in the pathogenic process.

papers.title: Biomimetic Nanomedicine for Aging‐Impaired Bone Regeneration: From Microenvironmental Dysfunction to Precision Therapeutics
papers.authors: Zeyu Wang; He Zhang; Simo Liu; Rui Wang; Yiran Wei; Kailu Zheng; Yanming Guo; Min Li; Dian Yuan; Yuxin Liu; Lifang Feng; Yongping Ma; Yan Liu
papers.abstract: Aging‐impaired bone regeneration represents a major clinical challenge due to diminished regenerative capacity and a progressively deteriorated microenvironment. This dysfunction arises from the interplay of cellular senescence, chronic inflammation driven by the senescence‐associated secretory phenotype (SASP), vascular insufficiency, and disrupted neuroregulation, collectively limiting effective bone repair. Conventional therapies, largely relying on single‐target interventions or passive delivery, remain insufficient to address these multifactorial barriers. Biomimetic nanomedicine offers a promising strategy by integrating biologically inspired designs with therapeutic cargos. Based on the principal biological feature emulated, these systems can be organized into four operational categories: cell‐derived, extracellular vesicle‐inspired, biomolecule‐inspired, and microenvironment‐inspired platforms. Biomimetic features dictate biological recognition, localization, retention, and stimulus responsiveness, whereas therapeutic cargos or active materials mediate downstream regenerative effects. To bridge this design‐based taxonomy with the biology of aging‐impaired bone repair, this review organizes current evidence within a pathology–design–outcome framework centered on four major pathological barriers: cellular dysfunction, osteoimmune dysregulation, vascular impairment, and disrupted neural regulation. This framework links age‐related pathological deficits with biomimetic design principles and regenerative outcomes, while highlighting key priorities for more precise and clinically translatable bone regeneration.

papers.title: Dual Control of Low-Density Lipoprotein Cholesterol Levels by ANGPTL3 and ANGPTL8
papers.authors: Xu, Y.; Luo, F.; Fletcher, J.; Inigo, M. M.; Burgess, S.; Liang, G.; Kinch, L. N.; Kozlitina, J.; Cohen, J. C.; Hobbs, H.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Inactivation of ANGPTL3 (angiopoietin-like protein 3, A3) is a proven therapeutic strategy for lowering plasma lipid levels independently of the LDL receptor (LDLR), yet the optimal approach to inactivate A3 remains unclear. A3 is proteolytically cleaved and circulates as full-length (A3-FL), N-terminal (A3-Nter) and C-terminal (A3-Cter) fragments. The specific contribution of each form of A3, and of its paralog, ANGPTL8 (A8), in modulating circulating levels of ApoB-Containing Lipoproteins (ABCLs) remain poorly defined. Clarifying these relationships will inform next-generation A3-directed therapies. METHODS: We performed liver perfusion studies to directly compare the number and composition of VLDL particles secreted from mice with and without A3. To amplify effects on cholesterol metabolism, we generated Ldlr-/- mice expressing wildtype A3 (A3-WT), A3-FL or A3-Nter, with or without co-expression of A8, and analyzed plasma lipids, circulating A3 and A8 complexes, and intravascular lipase activities. Complementary in vitro assays and structural modeling were used to assess relative endothelial lipase (EL) inhibition by A3 alone or in complex with A8. RESULTS: Liver perfusion studies revealed that A3 inactivation does not alter the rates of hepatic secretion of VLDL in wildtype or Ldlr-/- mice. Inactivation of A8 alone lowered plasma LDL-cholesterol (C) levels by ~20%, an effect dependent upon the expression of both EL and A3. Maximal inhibition of lipoprotein lipase (LPL) required co-expression of A8 plus both A3-FL and A3-Nter, indicating that A3 cleavage, in addition to A8 expression, is essential for maximal LPL inhibition. In contrast, A8 expression, but not A3 cleavage, was required for optimal EL inhibition. CONCLUSIONS: A8 acts in concert with A3 to differentially modulate LPL- and EL-mediated lipolysis, which antagonizes hepatic clearance of newly-secreted atherogenic ABCLs. This mechanistic framework refines our understanding of A3-targeted lipid lowering and highlights the therapeutic potential of dual A3- plus A8-directed strategies to treat dyslipidemia and prevent atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.

papers.title: Dual Role of Cx43 in Enhancing CDK4/6 Inhibitor Response and Promoting the Elimination of Therapy-Induced Senescent Tumor Cells
papers.authors: Carpintero-Fernandez, P.; Barturen-Gomez, M.; Alvarez, V.; Carneiro-Figueira, A.; Mazumdar, S.; De Chiara, L.; Garcia-Yuste, A.; Soler, M.; Bravo, S.; Mosquera, J.; Acea, B.; Fernandez-Lozano, C.; Caffarel, M. M.; Alabert, C.; Mayan, M. D.
papers.abstract: Breast cancer has become the most prevalent malignancy worldwide. A key clinical advance has been the introduction of cyclin-dependent kinase 4/6 inhibitors (CDK4/6i), that in combination with endocrine therapy has been a major advance for the treatment of luminal (ER/HER2-) breast cancer. CDK4/6i induce cell cycle arrest in G1 and cellular senescence improving clinical outputs. However, limited efficacy and therapeutic resistance remain major challenges due to incomplete effects or the failure to eliminate the accumulated tumor senescent cells. Here, we identify connexin 43 (Cx43), a membrane channel protein involved in cell-to-cell communication, identified as a novel target in luminal breast cancer that potentiates the effects of CDK4/6 inhibitors. We found that Cx43 not only reduces tumor cell proliferation by enhancing senescence but also reshapes the Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype (SASP) profile. We also demonstrate that, in combination with CDK4/6i, Cx43 reinforces G1 arrest via transcriptional downregulation of E2F targets including CDK4 and CDK6, and through interaction with p21/p27, deepens the senescent state. Importantly, the Cx43-associated senescent phenotype sensitizes tumor cells accumulated under CDK4/6i treatment to the senolytic agent Navitoclax. Our results demonstrate that upregulation of Cx43 in breast cancer reduces proliferation and enhances the clearance of therapy-induced senescent cells. The triple-drug strategy comprising CDK4/6i, Cx43 delivery, and a senolytic drug such as Navitoclax holds great promise for overcoming CDK4/6i resistance and improving clinical outcomes in ER/HER2- breast cancer and may also be applicable to other cancer types that respond to CDK4/6i or other pro-senescence antitumoral drugs.

papers.title: Erythrocyte aging links hypocalcemia to impaired flow dynamics and oxygen transport through volume dysregulation
papers.authors: Lim, J.; Tan, J. K. S.; Yuan, Y.; Chen, E. S. A.; Song, Y.; Tien, S. L.; Leo, H. L.; Kim, S.
papers.abstract: Red blood cells (RBCs) maintain their corpuscular volume through mechanotransducive ion-mediated processes in response to circulatory shear stress. However, with age, RBCs accumulate oxidative damage and undergo alterations in protein function, glucose metabolism and ion transport, raising fundamental questions about how volume homeostasis is preserved under mechanical load. Here, we investigated the differential responses of younger (YRBCs) and older RBCs (ORBCs) to fluid shear stress, with a focus on calcium-dependent regulation. We found that ORBCs exhibited a striking dependence on extracellular calcium to maintain volume stability. In calcium-depleted conditions, only ORBCs underwent pronounced post-shear swelling, with recovery only partially restored by ATP-dependent mechanisms. In contrast, calcium preserved volume homeostasis, identifying calcium-sensitive pathways as key compensatory regulators in metabolically compromised ORBCs. Notably, metabolically deficient YRBCs recapitulated the ORBC swelling phenotype, supporting a shift from ATP to calcium-dependent regulation with age. More importantly, shear-induced swelling impaired flow behaviour and oxygen delivery in ORBCs, linking defective volume control to microcirculatory dysfunction. Together, these findings potentially established calcium-dependent volume regulation as a critical adaptive mechanism in ageing RBCs and reveal a previously unrecognized hematological link to vascular dysfunction in hypocalcemia.

papers.title: First-Trimester Lipid Profile and Subsequent Gestational Diabetes Mellitus: A Retrospective Case–Control Study
papers.authors: Erinc Tekin; Askın Yıldız; Simge Tezel Yozgat
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is a common metabolic complication of pregnancy, and identifying women at increased risk early in gestation may facilitate closer surveillance and timely preventive strategies. This study aimed to investigate the association between first-trimester maternal lipid profile parameters and subsequent GDM and to evaluate their discriminatory performance for GDM. Methods: This retrospective case–control study included singleton pregnancies followed at İzmir Kâtip Çelebi University Atatürk Training and Research Hospital between January 2015 and December 2019. Serum lipid parameters obtained between 11 + 0 and 13 + 6 weeks of gestation were retrospectively retrieved and compared between women who subsequently developed GDM and those who did not. Associations with GDM were evaluated using binary logistic regression, and discriminatory performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis. Results: Of 367 women assessed for eligibility, 336 were included in the final analysis (201 with GDM and 135 controls). Women who developed GDM had higher triglyceride levels (median: 138 vs. 103 mg/dL; p 125 mg/dL yielded 62.69% sensitivity and 74.81% specificity. Conclusions: First-trimester maternal lipid alterations, particularly higher triglyceride levels, were associated with subsequent GDM. However, triglycerides demonstrated only modest discriminatory performance and should not be considered a stand-alone predictor. Routinely available lipid parameters may provide additional information for early GDM risk stratification.

papers.title: Glutaminolysis Shapes Cardiac Resilience to Stress via Mitochondrial Glutathione
papers.authors: Xinpei Wang; Jiaheng Zhou; Haomiao Bai; Zihan Wei; Lina Su; Changyang Xing; Guiling Wu; Min Li; Jiong An; Pengfei Zhang; Yi Zhang; Shifang Ding; Xing Zhang; Jingyi Ren; Feng Gao; Jia Li
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Cardiac reserve is a strong predictor of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, yet the metabolic mechanisms that enable the heart to mount an adaptive response to stress remain poorly understood. In this study, we sought to dissect the specific role of glutaminolysis, a key anaplerotic and redox-supporting pathway, in regulating cardiac reserve. METHODS: Cardiac reserve was assessed by echocardiography under β-adrenergic stimulation in mice with cardiomyocyte-specific deletion of glutaminase and in wild-type controls. Stable isotope tracing with [U- 13 C] glutamine was performed in Langendorff-perfused hearts. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial of acute glutamine supplementation in healthy volunteers was conducted to evaluate translational relevance (ChiCTR2400082676). RESULTS: During acute stress, such as exercise or β-adrenergic stimulation, glutaminolysis was rapidly mobilized to supply mitochondrial glutathione, preserving mitochondrial redox homeostasis and sustaining cardiac contractile reserve. Mice with cardiomyocyte-specific deletion of glutaminase exhibited marked impairments in both contractile reserve and exercise capacity, accompanied by a failure to elevate mitochondrial glutathione and consequent mitochondrial oxidative stress. Chronic exercise training upregulated cardiac glutaminase expression and expanded the mitochondrial glutathione pool, linking this adaptive mechanism to training-induced improvements in cardiac reserve. In humans, acute oral glutamine supplementation enhanced cardiac reserve, as assessed by exercise stress echocardiography, in a placebo-controlled crossover design. CONCLUSIONS: These findings reveal a novel metabolic paradigm in which glutaminolysis functions as a dynamic pathway supporting mitochondrial health and cardiac resilience, and highlight glutamine supplementation as a potential therapeutic strategy to enhance cardiac reserve.

papers.title: MitImpact 4: a genome-wide resource for the interpretation of coding and non-coding mitochondrial DNA variants
papers.authors: Agnese Giovannetti; Alessandro Napoli; Niccolò Liorni; Francesco Petrizzelli; Tommaso Biagini; Antonio Gasbarrini; Viviana Caputo; Tommaso Mazza
papers.abstract: Abstract Mitochondrial DNA variants are a frequent cause of inherited disease, yet their computational interpretation has focused almost exclusively on the 13 protein-coding genes. Variants in tRNA and rRNA genes, which carry a disproportionate share of the known pathogenic alleles, have remained a diagnostic blind spot, because their effect depends on RNA structure rather than on protein sequence and few dedicated predictors exist. MitImpact 4 removes this asymmetry. The database now covers all 49 704 single-nucleotide variants that can occur in the mitochondrial genome and reports their functional consequence, phylogenetic conservation, local mutational constraint, and population frequency in gnomAD, HelixMTdb, and ToMMo. Missense variants are annotated with APOGEE 2 and with newly added predictors, including AlphaMissense, ESM1b, VARITY, and LIST-S2, while tRNA and rRNA variants receive predictions from nAPOGEE, our RNA-specific model, alongside MitoTIP and PON-mt-tRNA. For both classes, scores are accompanied by posterior probabilities of pathogenicity that can be used within the ACMG/AMP framework for mitochondrial DNA. Clinical annotation from ClinVar and MITOMAP, including ClinGen expert-panel classifications, is integrated in a redesigned interface that also annotates user-submitted VCF files. MitImpact 4 is freely available at https://mitimpact.mcb2lab.org.

papers.title: Nutritional Assessment, Lipid Profile, Antioxidant Capacity, and Preliminary Toxicity Assessment of the Leaf Blade and Petiole of Xanthosoma sagittifolium (Taioba) from a Cultivar in Southeastern Brazil
papers.authors: Daniela Gomes de Moura; Ailton Junior Antunes da Costa; Dhionne Correia Gomes; Samuel Beiral Alves Pessoa; Rachel Oliveira Castilho; Renata Adriana Labanca; Marinalva Woods Pedrosa; Julio Onesio-Ferreira Melo; Raquel Linhares Bello de Araújo
papers.abstract: Non–conventional food plants (NCFPs) have gained attention as sustainable sources of nutrients and bioactive compounds, while their underutilized edible parts may contribute to food diversification and waste reduction. This study performed a descriptive comparative analysis of the nutritional, mineral, lipid, phenolic, antioxidant, oxalate, and acute toxicity profiles of Xanthosoma sagittifolium (Taioba) cultivated in Brazil. Samples were evaluated for proximate composition; minerals by ICP–OES; Folin–Ciocalteu reducing capacity; antioxidant capacity by ABTS, DPPH, and FRAP; fatty acid profile by GC–FID; oxalic acid content; and toxicity using the Artemia salina bioassay. The leaf blade showed substantially higher protein, total phenolic equivalents, FRAP capacity, and concentrations of several fatty acids, including α–linolenic and linoleic acids, as well as higher levels of most analyzed minerals. Conversely, the petiole exhibited markedly higher moisture, carbohydrates, and potassium. Both fractions demonstrated high dietary fiber content, a predominance of polyunsaturated fatty acids, and low atherogenicity and thrombogenicity indices. Although both fractions contained oxalates—with the leaf blade presenting nearly twice the concentration of the petiole—aqueous extracts of both parts showed no detectable acute lethality in the Artemia salina screening. Overall, the results highlight that Taioba represents a highly valuable nutritional resource. Furthermore, the integral utilization of both the leaf blade and the underutilized petiole offers a complementary, sustainable, zero–waste strategy for dietary diversification, provided that appropriate thermal processing is applied to mitigate oxalate concerns.

papers.title: P2X7 receptor-mediated inflammatory and ionic remodeling promotes atrial fibrillation in diabetes.
papers.authors: Yuntao Fu; Yuanjia Ke; Zhen Cao; Yuting Chen; Xiaojian Long; Yajia Li; Kexin Guo; Yixuan Luo; Kaigeng Hu; Qingyan Zhao
papers.abstract: AIMS: Diabetes mellitus (DM) is a major risk factor for atrial fibrillation (AF), yet the mechanisms by which diabetic metabolic stress promotes atrial arrhythmogenesis remain incompletely understood. Recent evidence suggests that purinergic signaling-driven sterile inflammation plays an important role in cardiac remodeling. This study aimed to investigate the role of the ATP-gated purinergic P2X7 receptor (P2X7R) in DM-associated AF and to explore its underlying mechanisms. METHODS AND RESULTS: Rats were randomly assigned to four groups: control (Con), diabetes mellitus (DM), P2X7R overexpression in controls (Con+P2X7), and P2X7R knockdown in diabetic rats (DM + P2X7 KD), with gene manipulation achieved using AAV9-cTnT vectors. AF susceptibility, atrial structural and electrical remodeling were systematically evaluated using electrophysiological studies, optical mapping, patch-clamp recordings, and molecular analyses. DM markedly increased AF inducibility and duration, accompanied by enhanced sympathetic nerve activity and activation of P2X7R-related inflammatory signaling. Compared with controls, DM atria exhibited pronounced interstitial fibrosis, connexin remodeling, delayed atrial activation, slowed conduction velocity, and increased conduction heterogeneity. Atrial P2X7R overexpression in control rats recapitulated key arrhythmogenic features, whereas P2X7R KD in diabetic rats significantly attenuated atrial remodeling and reduced AF susceptibility, without altering the diabetes-induced increase in sympathetic activity. At the cellular level, P2X7R selectively modulated INa, ICa,L, and IKur while relatively preserving Ito, and was associated with mitochondrial dysfunction and disturbed Ca2+ homeostasis, characterized by increased mitochondrial reactive oxygen species, loss of mitochondrial membrane potential, increased cytosolic Ca2+ signals, and reduced mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake. CONCLUSION: P2X7R-mediated inflammatory and mitochondrial signaling contribute to diabetic atrial remodeling and AF susceptibility. Targeting P2X7R may represent a potential therapeutic strategy for preventing AF in diabetes.

papers.title: Plant-Derived Bioactive Compounds, Cancer Stemness and Cellular Senescence: A Narrative Review of Preclinical Evidence and Translational Relevance to Cancer Recurrence and Drug Resistance
papers.authors: Sara Naseer; Wai-Yann Tan; Yin-Teng Sow; Zhi-Yin Wai; Sahana-Shri Ramanitharan; Paey-Ern Bay; Ching-Hsein Chen; Soi-Moi Chye
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Cancer recurrence and drug resistance arise from tumour-cell plasticity and microenvironmental adaptations that may persist after treatment. Cancer stem cells (CSCs) are associated with self-renewal, tumour initiation, residual disease, and treatment tolerance, whereas cellular senescence has context-dependent effects. Although therapy-induced senescence may restrict tumour-cell proliferation, persistent senescent tumour or stromal cells and their senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) can, in selected models, promote inflammatory signalling, stemness-associated phenotypes and therapeutic resistance. This narrative review critically evaluates preclinical and translational evidence concerning curcumin, resveratrol, epigallocatechin gallate, berberine, piperine and shikonin as potential adjunctive modulators of CSCs and senescence-associated processes. Methods: Relevant literature was identified through searches of the MEDLINE/PubMed database from June 2000 and July 2026, using terms related to plant-derived bioactive compounds, CSCs, cellular senescence, SASP, recurrence and drug resistance. Evidence was evaluated according to model relevance, exposure, functional validation and whether it represented direct cross-axis evidence, intermediate mechanistic evidence, or marker- and pathway-level support. Results: Most studies examined CSCs and senescence as separate processes. Direct evidence showing that the same compound, within the same cancer model, modifies a validated cancer stem-cell function and a defined senescence or SASP and subsequently reduces resistance or recurrence is limited or absent. Moreover, poor bioavailability, variable formulations, potentially unachievable experimental exposures, drug interactions, tumour heterogeneity and limited clinical evidence constrain translation. Conclusions: Future studies should incorporate pharmacologically relevant exposures, functional and longitudinal endpoints, causal validation and biomarker-guided combination designs to determine whether these compounds can safely complement standard anticancer therapies.

papers.title: Primary cilia mediate specific neuron-glia attachments in C. elegans through the secreted protein BUG-1.
papers.authors: Leland R Wexler; Brian Griffin; Priya Dutta; Piali Sengupta; Irina Kolotuev; Niels Ringstad; Maxwell G Heiman
papers.abstract: Primary cilia are signaling hubs that influence nearly every aspect of cell physiology. Neuronal primary cilia were recently found to form extensive attachments to glia in the mammalian brain, but it is not known how these attachments form or what functions they serve. Defects in cilia cause profound neurological disorders, highlighting the importance of understanding the specialized functions of neuronal cilia. Here, we use a genetic screen in Caenorhabditis elegans to determine how a stereotyped cilia-glia attachment forms and how the attachment affects ciliary calcium signaling. We find that two sensory neurons (URX and BAG) use their cilia to attach to a specific glial partner (ILsoL/R). This attachment requires BUG-1, a large secreted protein that localizes precisely to the cilia-glia attachment site. In the absence of BUG-1, neuronal cilia are present but always fail to attach to the glial cell. As a result, the URX cilia do not undergo activity-dependent remodeling seen in wild-type neurons and the BAG cilia exhibit reduced sensory stimulus-evoked calcium entry and defects in calcium clearance. Our work shows that cilia can select specific glial partners for attachment, identifies a novel protein that mediates these attachments, and demonstrates the functional consequences of loss of cilia-glia attachment on neuronal signaling. We propose that neuronal primary cilia act not only as antennae to receive long-range signals but also as points of close-range cell-cell contact, through which glia could modulate neuronal signaling.

papers.title: Scutellarein nanoparticles suppress colon cancer via PHB2-mediated mitophagy inhibition with modulatory effects on tumor-associated depression and osteotropic migration
papers.authors: Yuanzhi Li; Hao Xu; Zonglin Cai; Shimei Liu; Xuqiang Luo; Jinghua Liang; Yingying Liao
papers.abstract: Background Colorectal cancer progression involves mitophagy, in which Prohibitin 2 (PHB2) regulates the PARL–PGAM5–PINK1 axis. Scutellarein has antitumor activity but poor bioavailability. We developed integrin αvβ3-targeted β-cyclodextrin-based scutellarein nanoparticles (Scu-NPs), which enhance the solubility, stability, and tumor-targeting of scutellarein, and investigated whether they suppress colon cancer via PHB2-mediated mitophagy inhibition and modulate tumor-associated depression and osteotropic migration. Methods PHB2 expression and mitochondrial localization were examined in colon cancer cells. SW480 cells with PHB2 overexpression were treated with Scu or Scu-NPs. Proliferation, migration, invasion, apoptosis, mitochondrial function, and mitophagy-related proteins were assessed. Subcutaneous xenografts, a chronic unpredictable mild stress tumor–depression model, behavioral tests, osteotropic migration assays, and bioinformatics were used. Results PHB2 was highly expressed and mitochondria-localized in colon cancer cells. Scu-NPs downregulated PHB2, increased PARL, decreased PGAM5, PINK1, Parkin, and LC3-II/LC3-I, and increased P62, indicating mitophagy inhibition. Scu-NPs induced mitochondrial dysfunction, ROS accumulation, apoptosis, and inhibited proliferation, migration, and invasion; PHB2 overexpression partially reversed these effects. In vivo , Scu-NPs suppressed xenograft growth and improved depressive-like behaviors, with PHB2 overexpression attenuating these effects. In vitro , Scu-NPs reduced colon cancer cell migration toward osteoblast-conditioned medium, whereas PHB2 overexpression partially reversed this effect. Conclusion Scu-NPs suppress colon cancer by downregulating PHB2 and inhibiting mitophagy. PHB2 may serve as a shared molecular node linking tumor progression, depressive-like behaviors, and osteotropic migration, supporting Scu-NPs as a multi-target strategy.

papers.title: SphK1/S1P signaling network: From molecular mechanism to therapeutic targeting.
papers.authors: Duxiao Yang; Zhen Wang
papers.abstract: Sphingosine kinase 1 (SphK1) is a key rate-limiting enzyme in the sphingolipid metabolic network. It generates sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) by catalyzing the phosphorylation of Sphingosine (Sph). It plays a key regulatory role in various physiological and pathological processes such as cell proliferation, survival, migration, inflammatory response and immune regulation. SphK1 closely connects intracellular lipid metabolism with extracellular GPCR signaling network, forming a complex "inside-out" signal transduction system. In this review, we focus on the current understanding of SphK1, including its structure characteristics, activation mechanism and signal transduction pathway. We also review the roles of SphK1 pathway in tumor, inflammation and immunity, cardiovascular, nervous system, digestive system, respiratory system and metabolic disease. Establishing a correlation between SphK1 or the SphK1/S1P signal axis and targeted drugs such as inhibitors, agonists, even some natural Chinese medicines, provides important theoretical support for understanding the potential of SphK1 as a therapeutic target. Finally, we propose future research directions based on current advances and shortcomings.
